raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.1] [1. On the flesh of the viper.] Not all the fleshes of animals nourish a human being. Those of some are even deadly, no less than the drug-like substances which they call dēlētēria. Of the fleshes that do nourish us, some are foods and only that, while others, besides nourishing, also have the power as of a drug, since they alter the body by drying or moistening and by heating or cooling. At any rate, one can see plainly that the fleshes of vipers heat and dry when they are dressed as eels are, with oil, salts, dill, leek, and of course water in due measure. That they cleanse the whole body through the skin you may learn also from what I experienced when I was still young, in our Asia; I shall now go through each of these cases in order. A man ill with the affection called elephas for a time shared the same regimen with his household. But when, from association and intercourse with him, some of them came to share the affection, and he himself was by now foul-smelling and loathsome to look upon, they built a hut for him near the village on a low hill beside a spring and settled the man in it, bringing him each day as much food as was sufficient to live on. About the rising of the Dog Star, some wine was brought in an earthenware jar to reapers who were reaping near him; it was very fragrant. The man who brought it set it down near the reapers and went away. When the time for drinking came, their custom was to pour the wine out into a mixing-bowl and mix it with a moderate amount of water. But when a young man took up the jar and was drawing the wine out into the mixing-bowl, a dead viper fell out along with it. The reapers, fearing that they might suffer some harm from the drink, drank water themselves. As they were leaving, they made a present of the whole wine, ostensibly out of humanity, to the man ill with elephas, judging that it was better for him to be dead than to live in such a state. He, drinking from it, became healthy in a wonderful manner. For the whole lumpy part of his skin fell off like the covering of the soft-shelled animals, and what remained appeared quite soft, like that of crayfish and crabs when the shell around them has fallen off. Another such case arose from a similar chance occurrence in Asian Mysia, not far from our city. A man suffering from elephas set out to use naturally hot waters in the hope of benefit. He had a concubine, a slave, young and beautiful and with many lovers. To her the sick man entrusted various other affairs of the household, and in particular those of the storeroom. While he was using the waters they lodged in a house that had next to it a dry, squalid plot full of vipers. One of the vipers fell into a jar of wine that had been carelessly left lying and died in it. The concubine, considering this chance event a windfall, offered her master his drink from that jar. He, drinking it, was healed in the same way as the man in the hut. These two lessons you now have from the experience of chance occurrence; and besides them a third, from our imitation. For a man ill with this disease, more philosophical than the many, was terribly vexed by it and kept saying that it was better to be dead than to live. Since he was in so wretched a condition, I disclosed to him the two chance occurrences just related. He was himself experienced in bird-omens and had a friend wonderfully successful in this learning. Taking his seat with that friend to observe the birds, he was urged on to imitate what had been learned through experience, and by drinking wine drugged in this way he became leprous. Some time later we cured his lepra too with the usual drugs. A fourth man after this, who had made it his craft to catch live vipers, was at the beginning of that affection, and our purpose was that he should be cured as quickly as possible. So, having cut his vein and purged him with a drug that evacuates black bile, we advised him to make use of the vipers he caught, preparing them in a lopas as one does eels. This man, then, was treated in this way, the affection being breathed out of him through transpiration. Another man, a rich one, was not of our country but came from the middle of Thrace, a dream having urged him to Pergamum. The god then commanded him in a dream to drink each day of the drug made from vipers and to anoint his body from outside. Not many days later the affection changed into lepra, and this disease too was cured in its turn with the drugs the god ordered. So great a degree of drying power, then, does the flesh of vipers attain. But some of those who ate it were seized by a most violent thirst, and for this reason they call the vipers dipsades. There are also some who say that those bitten by them, though they drink, are not filled, but burst before they cease to thirst. For this reason I inquired of those in Rome who hunt vipers, whom they call Marsi, whether they had any sign to teach me that distinguishes the two kinds of vipers. They said that there is no kind of dipsas vipers at all. Rather, those that live by the sea and in places with much saline earth (halmyris) have briny flesh, and for this reason many such occur in Libya, but there are none in Italy because of the moistness of the land. These things, then, I heard the Marsi say, but I cannot state with certainty whether they speak the truth in everything or are also lying in some respect. That in the places they named some vipers occur which have salty flesh seems to me most plausible, for I know that the fleshes of animals change along with their foods. But I cannot declare that there is no kind of dipsas vipers. The safest course, then, is to take care not to hunt vipers in such places, whether for eating or for the preparation of a drug, such as this celebrated one which nearly all physicians call theriac. Now it is our custom, when we prepare the so-called theriac pastilles (artiskoi), to remove not only their head but also the tail. I have often reflected that the whole head is perhaps reasonably removed, on account of the venom contained in the mouth, but the tail unreasonably. Nor can one say that it must be done so on account of the residues of the food, both the moist and the dry. For having killed them, then flayed them and laid them open, we take out and throw away all the inner parts, so that only the substance of the fleshes is left, together with the arteries and veins that grow through it. These have a very small bulk relative to the whole flesh and are not even visible unless one inspects very carefully. The pastilles, then, which they also name theriac pastilles, we prepare thus. Taking the vipers cleaned, we boil them in water until they seem to us to be exactly boiled. We put dill into the water along with them right from the start. After the boiling we separate the spines from the fleshes, and then mix the flesh with ground bread. This bread we do not take at random, but the purest possible, well baked in an oven (klibanos), with a moderate amount of salt and leaven. We dry it beforehand in a dry room without moisture, until it becomes dry enough to be pounded in a mortar. Yet we do not mix it in by pounding it, but by soaking it in the water in which we boiled the vipers. The flesh itself, before mixing it with the bread, we triturate in a cooks' mortar until it becomes exactly smooth. After this, having moulded small thin pastilles, we dry them in a warm and dry room and keep them, storing them again in such a room. These we prepare at the onset of summer, when the flesh of vipers is at its very best. Later we use them by pounding and sifting them, then triturating them again and mixing them with salts prepared for pleasantness of taste; we also put them into the theriac. At the same season the salts made from roasted vipers are also prepared. We throw the vipers alive into a new pot together with the drugs strewn underneath and laid around them, all of which it is not the business of the present treatise to state now. Indeed, someone might perhaps reasonably reproach us even over the preparation of the pastilles, as having gone through it out of place. But since these things have already been said, let them stand, even if they seem not altogether proper to the present treatise. What follows, let it be said in fitting measure. It is fitting to recall, concerning the general power of the flesh of vipers, that it is drying and strongly dispersing, while heating moderately. Its power, it seems, presses towards the skin, and through the skin it moves the residues in the body. So a not inconsiderable multitude of lice is generated in those who have abundant kakochymia in their bodies. Also, the so-called epidermis separates from the skin and falls off like a husk; it is in the epidermis that the thick and earthy humours, among those carried to the skin, are more held back, and by these psōrai, leprai and elephantes arise. This, then, is what I had to tell you about the fleshes of the viper; next I shall take up the account again. The fleshes of animals that are hotter by nature not only nourish us but also heat, while those of colder animals cool. In the same way, those of drier animals dry, and those of moister animals moisten. Remember, then, what you learned in the work On Mixtures. When you recognise that some animal is drier in mixture, as for instance the wild boar than the domestic pig, know that its flesh too is more drying. The same holds for the other differences of mixtures: for example, the sheep is drier than the pig, the goat than the sheep, the ox than the goat, and the lion than the ox. So too in respect of heat, the lion is hotter than the dog, the dog than the bull, and the bull than the ox whose testicles have been cut out. In proportion, then, to their excess in mixture over the other animals, their fleshes will also differ. For this reason, when you wish to dry the body, you will give the flesh of animals drier in mixture; when you want to heat it, that of hotter ones; when you undertake to make it colder, that of colder ones; and when moister, that of moister ones. No small difference among the fleshes lies also in some of them having been salted. For they differ altogether, so that often the salted flesh of an animal most moist in mixture is far more drying than the unsalted flesh of one dry by nature. And the roasted flesh is drier than that boiled in water. Some have also written that the fleshes of other animals benefit when eaten and when applied to the affected parts. One example is the flesh of the land hedgehog, dried, if it is drunk by those with elephantiasis, cachectics, those subject to spasms and nephritics, and further by those who have the dropsy called anasarca. If it is of a nature to do these things, its power would be strongly dispersing and drying, as is that of the dried weasel, which indeed benefits epileptics when drunk. They say that the flesh of salted cats, ground and applied, draws out splinters, evidently as having a drawing power. They also say that the flesh of mussels (myakes) suits ulcers caused by a biting dog. I, however, find no special power that ulcers of this kind require, as those produced by the bite of a rabid dog do. The flesh of snails too, first pounded in a mortar and afterwards triturated, becomes the most drying of all for parts having superfluous moisture, so that it suits the dropsical as well. The moisture from them, taken alone by itself without the flesh, is called by most people snail's mucus. Mixed with frankincense or aloe or myrrh, or some or all of these, until it has the thickness of a cerate, it becomes a glue-like drug and dries the purulent mucous discharges of the ears well. Applied on the forehead, it is also a drying adhesive application (anakollēma) against fluxes into the eyes. Some also use the snails for splinters, triturating them whole with their shells, and there are some who use them for checking the menses. The fleshes alone I myself once triturated and applied, in the country, to a wound that had occurred together with a wounding and crushing of a nerve. The wound was glued together well and the nerve did not become inflamed. The man was tough and rustic; I mixed with the fleshes, as they were being triturated, fine flour-dust, taking it from the wall next to the mill. Some of the physicians before us have written that one ought to mix myrrh or frankincense with them for such a use, but I had neither of these, being outside the city on the country estate. One could also mix in ground roasted resin, if it is to hand. Whenever you wish to obtain much of the snails' mucus by itself, prick their flesh with a stylus. response.translation: [11.1.2] [2. On fat and suet.] Fat (pimelē) and suet (stear). These too are among the commonest of the parts in animals. For all well-nourished animals have fat or suet, whereas lean and ill-nourished ones often appear to have none at all, and often have so little, and that so dry, that it is hard to use. Suet differs from fat in thickness; for this reason suet arises in animals whose whole nature is more earthy, just as fat does in those whose nature is more moist. For this very reason, then, fat melts easily under fire, but once melted does not easily congeal; suet, by contrast, does not melt easily, and if it is melted it congeals very quickly and appears much harder than fat. The pig, then, when well nourished, has a very great deal of fat on account of the natural moistness of its mixture, whereas oxen and goats and all other horned animals produce suet in greatest quantity on account of their dryness. You may, if you wish, call the whole oleaginous and oily substance in animals suet, as most physicians do; and you may also name this whole kind fat. You may not, however, if you wish not to speak falsely, say that the suet of goats is moister than that of pigs. For the latter is the moistest of nearly all the others, and for this reason in its action it is close to oil in power, though it is more softening than oil and more concoctive. And for this reason it is mixed into the poultices suited to inflammations. But for those who are bitten in the region of the rectum or the colon we inject goat's rather than pig's suet, not because it is more blunting of pungency (for, so far as its nature goes, pig's suet blunts more, and for this reason it is also mixed into drugs that treat ulcers, such as the one called parygron), but because goat's suet congeals easily on account of its thickness, whereas pig's flows away just like oil; for this reason we inject the former rather in dysenteric and tenesmic patients, when we wish to soothe their biting. Some things also blunt pungencies more on account of fineness of particles, when what is giving pain lies in the depth of the bodies that are being bitten. For the coarse-particled passes less, and the fine-particled more, through whole bodies, and mixes itself with all the biting ichors. In this respect, at any rate, goose suet blunts more effectively what bites in the depth of bodies. It is also hotter than pig's. Between them lies that of cocks; and that of male animals is always hotter and drier. Among these themselves, that of those whose testicles are excised is less hot and dry; for the castrated male always comes to resemble the females of the same kind. The general heading of the account, which must be remembered, is this: that the differences of the fat or suet in animals (or however you wish to name this whole kind of oleaginous and oily body in animals) always arise according to the mixture of the animals. Since, then, the pig falls short in heat and dryness of nearly all four-footed animals, for this reason it also has fat that is both less hot and more moist. Now the power of all fat is moistening and heating of human bodies; for this must be remembered throughout, having been stated at the beginning of this treatise; and the differences in each of them are matters of more and less. For the fat of the pig, relative to us, has moistening in abundance, but heating not in the same way as oil; rather, the fat (lipos) of pigs is on a level with the heat in us. That of bulls is much hotter and drier than that of pigs, we again remembering here too that the male is always drier and hotter than the female, and that the castrated male resembles the female, as indeed does everything young; and that among the young themselves the female is moister and less hot than the male. Thus calf's suet falls short of that of bulls in heat and dryness, and that of kids of that of goats, and that of goats falls short of that of he-goats, and again that of bulls in turn falls short of that of lions; for that is the most dispersing of nearly all those in quadrupeds. For it is also the hottest of them and the most fine-particled, so that if you mix it into the drugs suited to ulcers and inflammations, you will not only do no good but will even do harm, having made the drug more pungent than is fitting. But for chronic hardened swellings, contractures (ankylai) of sinews, and in short whatever is scirrhous, it is most suitable, in cases in which that of pigs appears most ineffective. That of bulls stands roughly equally distant from each, being as much hotter and drier than that of pigs as it falls short of that of lions. As being placed in the middle, then, it is reasonably mixed into each kind of drug, both those that treat scirrhous conditions and those that concoct inflamed parts, such as the one called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax, resin, pitch and suet. For into this, whether you put bull's or calf's or he-goat's or goat's or pig's, you will make a suppurative and concoctive drug. But pig's, when put in, suits children and women and, in a word, the soft-fleshed, while bull's is useful for diggers, reapers and all who have hard flesh, whether through their natural mixture or through the kind of life they lead. All suet, as it ages, becomes hotter and more fine-particled than it was, and so also more dispersing. This holds for nearly all things that age, at least those that do not rot first. For wine, honey, vinegar, cheese, butter and oesypum, and every oil, whether mastic oil or castor oil or radish oil or the very oil from olives, become thinner and more fine-particled as they age, and for this reason appear more pungent to those who taste them and more dispersing to those who use them, in all hardened and hard-to-resolve affections. I, then, have said that they appear more pungent to those who taste them. But some of those who corrupt the meanings of words call all such things not pungent but astringent, even down to pepper, as if it made no difference whether one says astringent or pungent. And if you ask them in turn about oak-galls, myrtles, medlars, pomegranate rinds, omphakion and sumach, they say that these too are astringent, although the perception we have from them is the most opposite to that which arises in us from pepper, pyrethron, mustard, euphorbium, onion, garlic and adarce. If, then, just as they apply the name of astringency in common to both of the affections arising in us in taste, so too they think that the affections themselves have a single nature, they must be considered anything rather than human beings, as alone possessing senses peculiar to themselves. But if they agree that unripe grape, sumach, oak-gall, balaustion and hypocistis draw together and constrict our substance, while pepper, mustard and pyrethron separate, bite and pass through it, then they improperly name the biting and heating things astringent, but they have not erred in their knowledge of the drugs themselves. If one must say by conjecture whether they err in the names or in the things, I for my part would say that these men have erred rather in the names, and especially those unaccustomed to the Greek tongue, such as Dioscorides of Anazarbus, who has said many things well among the matters recorded concerning medical material, but is ignorant of the meanings of Greek words. When this man, then, says that the suet of goats is more astringent than that of pigs, if by 'more astringent' he wishes to indicate 'more pungent', we shall accept the statement as true; but if he means what has the kind of quality and power that sumach and rhēon, hypocistis and balaustion have, we shall say that the statement is not true. Since they also say that the suet of vipers, when someone plucks out the hairs in the armpits by the roots and anoints the place, prevents these from growing again, I thought it better to test this too, and having done as they bade I found them to be lying, as also in the claim that it cures the beginnings of hypochyses. That the suet of bears suits alopecias they wrote truly, but we have more approved drugs than it for the affection. As for that of foxes, however, when they say that it treats earaches without distinguishing what sort of earaches they mean, as men who do not even know articulately what they are saying, one should not pay any attention to them at all. Others praise the suet of fishes, as being for hypochyses or whatever affection they wish to name. Others again write not simply of fishes, but of river fishes, and others rather of sea fishes, so that they may seem to know something more than the many.

raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.15] [15. On castoreum.] The testicles of the beaver they call castoreum. It is a celebrated drug with many uses, so much so that Archigenes wrote a whole book on the use of castoreum. He went through its particular powers one by one. I, as with the other drugs, so with this one too, shall state its general power; by looking to this, one will be able to discover the particular ones for oneself. That it heats is quite evident. For if you grind it exactly smooth, moisten it with oil, and then anoint and rub some part with it, you will clearly perceive the part being heated. All things that heat, by dispersing some of the substance that lies near them, at once also dry it. The exception is something moist by nature, such as oil and water, which takes on an acquired hot quality and not a power, as these very things do when brought near fire or the summer sun. Castoreum, then, since its consistency is dry and it has also acquired the capacity to heat, reasonably dries. This it has in common with very many other drugs. But it is sufficiently fine-particled, and in this respect it is more powerful than other drugs that heat and dry to the same degree as it does. For fine-particled drugs are more active than coarse-particled ones, even if they have an equal power, because they pass through and go into the depth of the bodies they come into contact with, especially when these are dense, as the sinewy ones are. At any rate, such parts are clearly greatly benefited by castoreum for the stated cause. Most physicians, however, are ignorant of this. In using castoreum they attend only to the fact that some part trembles or is convulsed, or is insensible or motionless, or has impaired sensation or impaired motion. They do not know that such symptoms follow unlike conditions of the body. But you have learnt from Hippocrates that convulsion arises both from repletion and from evacuation. Where it is necessary to evacuate what is contained in the nerves contrary to nature, give castoreum to drink and also apply it externally upon the skin. But where convulsion arises through excessive dryness, know that this drug is most contrary. By the same reasoning it is most beneficial to those who tremble through plethos, but most contrary to those who fall into such an affection through evacuation. Analogously to the affections mentioned, I found and distinguished the condition of the hiccup that arises in the stomach. If the patients suffer this from plethos, proceed to the use of castoreum; but if it arises through dryness and evacuation, or through the biting of pungent fluids, avoid the drug. Now someone attending to its smell and taste might suspect that it has a substance most alien to the human body. In use, however, it appears to do none of the things that such substances do, some of them harming the stomach, others the belly, others the head, others some other part. This drug, by contrast, displays great benefit and inflicts no harm whatever on any part. This holds whether you apply it to a moist body needing dryness, or to a cold one needing heat, or to a moist and cold one requiring heat and dryness. It holds especially when the person is without fever. It holds also for those who are feverish, but not very hotly, having rather what one might call a lukewarm fever, such as occurs above all in kataphorai and lethargies. We have given castoreum to very many people, together with white pepper, a spoonful's quantity of each, given to drink in honey-water, and no one was harmed in any way. When the menses were retained, I first evacuated moderately from the ankle, then gave castoreum with pennyroyal or kalaminthē. I always found that the drug set purgation in motion, without the woman being harmed at all. It also expels retained afterbirths. All these things, then, it accomplishes when drunk in honey-water. Some people are intractably inflated in the belly, or suffer gripes, or hiccup, from cold and viscid humours or from thick and flatulent pneuma. These it benefits when drunk in oxycrate. response.translation: [11.1.15] [15. On castoreum.] The testicles of the beaver they call castoreum. It is a celebrated drug with many uses, so much so that Archigenes wrote a whole book on the use of castoreum. He went through its particular powers one by one. I, as with the other drugs, so with this one too, shall state its general power; by looking to this, one will be able to discover the particular ones for oneself. That it heats is quite evident. For if you grind it exactly smooth, moisten it with oil, and then anoint and rub some part with it, you will clearly perceive the part being heated. All things that heat, by dispersing some of the substance that lies near them, at once also dry it. The exception is something moist by nature, such as oil and water, which takes on an acquired hot quality and not a power, as these very things do when brought near fire or the summer sun. Castoreum, then, since its consistency is dry and it has also acquired the capacity to heat, reasonably dries. This it has in common with very many other drugs. But it is sufficiently fine-particled, and in this respect it is more powerful than other drugs that heat and dry to the same degree as it does. For fine-particled drugs are more active than coarse-particled ones, even if they have an equal power, because they pass through and go into the depth of the bodies they come into contact with, especially when these are dense, as the sinewy ones are. At any rate, such parts are clearly greatly benefited by castoreum for the stated cause. Most physicians, however, are ignorant of this. In using castoreum they attend only to the fact that some part trembles or is convulsed, or is insensible or motionless, or has impaired sensation or impaired motion. They do not know that such symptoms follow unlike conditions of the body. But you have learnt from Hippocrates that convulsion arises both from repletion and from evacuation. Where it is necessary to evacuate what is contained in the nerves contrary to nature, give castoreum to drink and also apply it externally upon the skin. But where convulsion arises through excessive dryness, know that this drug is most contrary. By the same reasoning it is most beneficial to those who tremble through plethos, but most contrary to those who fall into such an affection through evacuation. Analogously to the affections mentioned, I found and distinguished the condition of the hiccup that arises in the stomach. If the patients suffer this from plethos, proceed to the use of castoreum; but if it arises through dryness and evacuation, or through the biting of pungent fluids, avoid the drug. Now someone attending to its smell and taste might suspect that it has a substance most alien to the human body. In use, however, it appears to do none of the things that such substances do, some of them harming the stomach, others the belly, others the head, others some other part. This drug, by contrast, displays great benefit and inflicts no harm whatever on any part. This holds whether you apply it to a moist body needing dryness, or to a cold one needing heat, or to a moist and cold one requiring heat and dryness. It holds especially when the person is without fever. It holds also for those who are feverish, but not very hotly, having rather what one might call a lukewarm fever, such as occurs above all in kataphorai and lethargies. We have given castoreum to very many people, together with white pepper, a spoonful's quantity of each, given to drink in honey-water, and no one was harmed in any way. When the menses were retained, I first evacuated moderately from the ankle, then gave castoreum with pennyroyal or kalaminthē. I always found that the drug set purgation in motion, without the woman being harmed at all. It also expels retained afterbirths. All these things, then, it accomplishes when drunk in honey-water. Some people are intractably inflated in the belly, or suffer gripes, or hiccup, from cold and viscid humours or from thick and flatulent pneuma. These it benefits when drunk in oxycrate. Whatever it benefits when taken into the body, it also benefits when applied upon the skin together with Sicyonian or old oil. Conditions needing more heat should also be rubbed with it on its own. It also benefits if one burns it as a fumigation on coals and draws it in by inhalation, especially for the moist and cold affections of the lung and brain. All lethargic and kataphoric affections accompanied by fevers, however, are better treated not by moistening it with one of the oils mentioned, but rather by applying it with rose oil to the head and the neck.

response.translation: [11.1.27] [27. On the cuttlefish.] The shell of the cuttlefish is quite porous, not stony like those of oysters. Cleansing, then, it has in common with them, as do the other shells of the testaceans, just as it also has drying. But the fine-particled nature of its substance belongs to it as a special property beyond the others; for this reason we also use it burnt for alphoi, ephelis, phakoi (lentil-spots) and psorai. Moreover, mixed with mined salt, it melts away the pterygia that arise on the eyes. And even before it is burnt, when roasted and ground smooth, it brightens the teeth and dries ulcers. We are also accustomed to use the moderate degree of its roughness against the great roughnesses in the eyes which they call sykōseis: we carve out of it something resembling a collyrium in shape and rub them with it so as to draw blood. For when this has been done, the reducing collyria also act better upon them.

response.translation: [11.1.29] [29. On oesypous wool.] Wool that is still dirty, and for this reason called by some 'oesypous', usefully takes up the embrocations applied to parts that have been bruised or struck in any way whatever, and it contributes to the benefit derived from them on account of its oesypum. Wool that has been washed and no longer has its oesypum becomes a suitable material for taking up the liquids poured over it. When burnt, it has a power that is pungent and hot, together with a fine-particled nature, so that it very quickly melts away even flabby flesh in ulcers. It is also put into a drying drug. Burn it as you burn most other things: fill a new pot, then close it with a lid that has several holes.

response.translation: [11.1.33] [33. On snails.] Whole snails, burnt together with their shells, with omphacitis gall and white pepper mixed in with them, are of great benefit in dysenteries, in those cases where the ulcers are not yet putrefying. There should be one part of the pepper, two of the gall, and four of the ash of the snails. Having made these thoroughly smooth, sprinkle them on the cooked dishes and give them to drink in water or in wine that is white and harsh. Apart from being mixed with gall, the ash of snails is of a sufficiently drying power, which also has something of heat on account of the burning. Unburnt snails, ground smooth together with their shells, are applied both over the whole belly in the dropsical and over the swellings in the joints in the arthritic. Their application becomes hard to remove, but it dries sufficiently. And indeed it is proper to let them remain applied the whole time, until they fall off of their own accord. This is to be done also in the case of swellings from a blow that are hard to resolve, and with a contusion that has occurred in the ears. For they sufficiently dry all of these, even if a viscous and thick fluid is contained in the depth.

raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.34] [34. On burnt crabs.] The ash of river crabs is drying, like the things mentioned before, but by a property of its whole substance it acts wonderfully in those bitten by a rabid animal, both on its own and, much more, together with gentian and frankincense. There should be one part of the frankincense, five of the gentian and ten of the crabs. On occasion, and rarely, we have used them burnt in other ways, but for the most part in the way that Aeschrion the Empiricist used them, an old man most experienced in drugs, our fellow citizen and teacher. It was a dish of red copper, on which he placed the crabs alive and burned them until they were reduced to ash, so that they could easily be ground fine. This Aeschrion always had the drug prepared and ready in his house, burning the crabs in the summer season, after the rising of the Dog Star, when the sun was in Leo and the moon was in its eighteenth day. He gave this drug to drink every day to those bitten by a rabid animal, up to the fortieth day, sprinkling a good-sized spoonful into water. But if he took charge of the bitten person not from the beginning but some days after the bite, he sprinkled in two spoonfuls each day. On the wound itself he also used the plaster drug made with Bruttian pitch, opopanax and vinegar, which takes one litra of pitch, one Italian xestes of the most pungent vinegar, and three ounces of opopanax. Although these things do not belong to the present treatise, I have written them because of my confidence in the drug, since no one of those who used it in the way described has ever died. I shall also compose separately another treatise on the things that act by a property of the whole substance, among which are all things of this kind. One must therefore pardon the untimeliness of the writing, both now and in other places of this treatise where it sometimes occurs, on account of the benefit from what is said, which is very great, and which I wish to be preserved for the people after us, even if death intervening should prevent me from writing the next parts of this treatise. Our teacher Pelops, wishing to state the causes of all such things, said that the crab, being an aquatic animal, reasonably benefits those bitten by a rabid animal, who are in fear of being seized by lytta, a most dry affection, which is why they also fear water. He said that river crabs, not sea crabs, are suitable, since because of the admixture of salts, which are most drying, sea animals would not preserve an exact contrariety to lytta. And when someone said to him, 'Why then do not all the animals in drinkable water benefit similarly to the crabs?', 'Because,' he said, 'they cannot receive a preparation similar to that of the crabs. For when these are burnt, their ash, becoming drying, both consumes and at the same time disperses the venom of the biting dogs.' These, then, were the things Pelops said, professing and priding himself on knowing the causes of them all. But I, unless I first persuade myself that I know something exactly, do not attempt to persuade my neighbours. Accordingly I did not accept Pelops' argument as true either, since it is open to many objections, but I hold that the crabs too benefit by the property of the whole substance. But because none of those who used them has died, I wished this to have been made clear by me already, with the whole bodies at any rate, even if it is not proper to the present treatise. It was a dish of red copper, on which he placed the crabs alive and burned them until they were reduced to ash, so that they could easily be ground fine. This Aeschrion always had the drug prepared and ready in his house, burning the crabs in the summer season, after the rising of the Dog Star, when the sun was in Leo and the moon was in its eighteenth day. He gave this drug to drink every day to those bitten by a rabid animal, up to the fortieth day, sprinkling a good-sized spoonful into water. But if he took charge of the bitten person not from the beginning but some days after the bite, he sprinkled in two spoonfuls each day. On the wound itself he also used the plaster drug made with Bruttian pitch, opopanax and vinegar, which takes one litra of pitch, one Italian xestes of the most pungent vinegar, and three ounces of opopanax. Although these things do not belong to the present treatise, I have written them because of my confidence in the drug, since no one of those who used it in the way described has ever died. I shall also compose separately another treatise on the things that act by a property of the whole substance, among which are all things of this kind. One must therefore pardon the untimeliness of the writing, both now and in other places of this treatise where it sometimes occurs, on account of the benefit from what is said, which is very great, and which I wish to be preserved for the people after us, even if death intervening should prevent me from writing the next parts of this treatise. Our teacher Pelops, wishing to state the causes of all such things, said that the crab, being an aquatic animal, reasonably benefits those bitten by a rabid animal, who are in fear of being seized by lytta, a most dry affection, which is why they also fear water. He said that river crabs, not sea crabs, are suitable, since because of the admixture of salts, which are most drying, sea animals would not preserve an exact contrariety to lytta. And when someone said to him, 'Why then do not all the animals in drinkable water benefit similarly to the crabs?', 'Because,' he said, 'they cannot receive a preparation similar to that of the crabs. For when these are burnt, their ash, becoming drying, both consumes and at the same time disperses the venom of the biting dogs.' These, then, were the things Pelops said, professing and priding himself on knowing the causes of them all. But I, unless I first persuade myself that I know something exactly, do not attempt to persuade my neighbours. Accordingly I did not accept Pelops' argument as true either, since it is open to many objections, but I hold that the crabs too benefit by the property of the whole substance. But because none of those who used them has died, I wished this to have been made clear by me already, with the whole bodies at any rate, even if it is not proper to the present treatise. For this was not what was proposed.

raw_text: {"translation": "[11.1.49] [49. On the sea dragon and the red mullet.] Some have written that the following animals, split open alive and applied at once to the affected parts, are beneficial: the sea dragon placed upon its own sting, and likewise the red mullet upon that of the sea dragon; house mice upon that of the scorpion, as also the lizard; the shrew-mouse upon its own bite, and the Chalcidian lizard, which they also give to drink in wine, as healing its own bite. They have written too that the scorpion thoroughly heals its own sting when applied ground smooth, and likewise when eaten roasted. They say that it is also suited to those bitten by a viper, and the gecko to those stung by a scorpion. They say also that in the districts of Egypt the so-called aseirakos, dried, is given to those stung by a scorpion, and that the so-called kybion is usefully employed for the bite of a dog, applied over the wound; and many other such things, about which we shall speak at greater length in the discussion of things that act by a peculiarity of the whole substance. Some of the physicians of our time have used the oil in which whole animals have been boiled. response.translation: [10.2.1] On the fluids in animals. [1. On blood.] Blood: one must of course understand in addition 'of an animal in its natural state', for this is what is truly blood. Melancholic, bitter-bilious, phlegmatic, serous or putrefactive blood is mixed, composed of blood in the true sense and of the humour and ichor that have been mixed with it. And of natural blood itself, in each animal some is moister and some drier, and some more and some less hot; for no blood is cold.

[10.2.2] [2. On pig's blood.] Pig's blood, then, is moist and less hot, and most closely resembles human blood in its mixture, since the flesh of pigs too resembles that of humans. Indeed, we already know of many innkeepers and cooks who were caught selling human flesh as pork, and yet none of those who ate it perceived any difference. Moreover, I heard trustworthy people relate that in a certain inn they had eaten abundant broth with most delicious meat, and when they had already eaten their fill, they found in it the front part of a finger, at the nail itself. Fearing that the people in the inn might eat them too, as being accustomed to the practice, they left at once, vomited up what they had eaten, and continued their journey. They also said that not long afterwards the people at the inn were caught for the human beings they used to slaughter. So one might reasonably suppose that the blood of pigs too is most similar to that of humans. For it is from such blood that the flesh has both its first generation and its nourishment thereafter. Hence whoever says that human blood is useful against some disease, let him first demonstrate in pig's blood, if not the same action, at least a similar one. For even if it should fall short of human blood in some respect of its power, it will at any rate do something comparable, and once this is known we shall expect the benefit from human blood to be more complete. But if it appears to preserve not even a little of what is promised, there is no reason to make trial of human blood either. For we have found by experience that similar things are productive of similar effects. At any rate, among us in Pergamum, and indeed throughout almost the whole of Asia, those who have trepanned fractured bones of the head are accustomed to pour dove's blood onto the thick membrane [κατασχεῖν, probably to be read καταχεῖν]. Then someone who happened to have a wood-pigeon but not a dove used the wood-pigeon's blood, and the man was nevertheless saved. And another, using the blood of a turtle-dove on another patient, did the man no harm. For to use similar things for the same affections when those tested beforehand are not available is one of the things agreed upon and attested by experience. And indeed most of human life is carried on in this way.

He himself recommends, after the use of that blood, sprinkling on either chalcanthum or hemlock seed. And he says that when people do this the hairs either do not grow at all or grow downy, as though in applying the hemlock seed he were applying some trifling drug, and one not capable by itself of vigorously chilling whatever parts it is placed on. Some also smear the bat's blood on the genitals of boys, thinking that by this they will keep the parts without pubic hair for a very long time. And yet they ought to think not 'for a very long time', but that the parts will remain so permanently, just as they suppose of the armpits too. Now it is reasonable that something of this sort should come about from the part's being strongly chilled; but the bat's blood is not cold in potency to such a degree, for no blood at all is cold. As food, however, many people often use the blood of the hare, of hens and of goats: the blood of the hare and of hens not a few even of those in the cities, and that of goats those in the countryside, who fill the goats' stomachs with it together with the fat, as Homer said of the suitors. But our present discussion is not about things administered in the role of food, but about those administered as drugs. Some things, as was also said earlier, are at once foods and drugs, and of these we speak in this treatise insofar as they are drugs, not insofar as they are foods. For those who have given goat's blood with honey to dropsical patients administer it as a drug, not as a food, and so too those who have used it roasted for dysentery or for a flux of the belly. raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.5] [5. raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.8] [8. On the whey of milk.] Whey, as has been said, has a cleansing power. [10.2.13] [13. On bile.] This humour has been shown to be the hottest of the humours in each animal. Just as animals have blood and flesh that are unlike in their mixture, so by the same reasoning they also have unlike bile. For in the hottest animals the bile too must necessarily exceed the biles of the other animals, while in those less hot than these this humour too falls short in proportion, by as much as it falls short in the other things as well. For you have learned that all the humours in each of the blooded animals are four: blood, phlegm, and yellow and black bile. You have also learned that it is the custom not only of physicians but of all the Greeks to call yellow bile simply 'bile', on the understanding that the hearers will supply the name of the colour, but not to call black bile simply 'bile'; instead, with this whole addition, they call it 'black bile'. You also know that they sometimes call yellow bile 'pale yellow', and that in the bladder on the liver we see it in the dissections of animals sometimes pale yellow and sometimes yellow. You have also heard that yellow bile is hotter than pale yellow bile by as much as it is also thicker. For when a serous moisture is mixed with yellow bile, the pale yellow comes to be, just as the pale yellow, when heated further, is rendered thick in consistency and yellow in colour. And indeed in animals too it appears yellow in those that are hotter and pale yellow in those that are less so. And whenever hot animals happen to have gone hungry and thirsty, it turns towards the dark colour: sometimes this is verdigris-like, sometimes dark blue, and sometimes that of woad, which is duskier than that of cabbage. Pay attention, then, you too, to the colour of the biles whenever you prepare a drug in which some bile is also contained. Into the so-called kykliskoi and trochiskoi, such as that of Andron, of Polyeides, of Pasion and that of Bitinus, they mix the bile of the bull. When they prepare drugs useful for the eyes, they use that of the hyena, the cock, the partridge and certain other animals. The bull's bile is evidently hotter and more drying than that of castrated oxen. For the castrated animal always comes to resemble the female and the young. Just as these exceed the mature in moisture but fall short in heat, in the same way the castrated ox falls short of bulls. And I have seen the bile of some bulls dark blue, the yellow having been over-roasted; I did not think fit to put it into the drug being prepared, but chose the moderately yellow bile of another bull. For that bull had been exhausted by excessive toil, being dragged with violent bonds, so that it is quite clear that, having also been enraged in this work, it had a hotter mixture. It was likely too that it had been thirsty and hungry while being dragged violently. To speak in summary: just as urine appears moderately pale yellow with moderate drinking, yellow in those who have been thirsty, have gone without food and have toiled much, and white in those who have been filled and become drunk, so bile too changes its colours, towards the yellower in exercises, fasting and thirst, and towards the whiter in the opposite conditions. Know then that if you put markedly yellow bile into the drug being prepared, you will make it hotter; if pale yellow bile, moderately hot; and if bile that is slack and watery, falling short of the appropriate mixture by as much as the bile has turned towards the whiter. In this way, then, for those who open closed haemorrhoids by means of bull's bile, it has sometimes appeared weak and sometimes pungent beyond what is appropriate. Some difference also arises from the body that uses the bile, according as it is sensitive or insensitive, readily affected or not readily affected. But from the bile itself, as I said, the variation is not small. At any rate the same person is bitten more by yellow bile and less by pale yellow. It is possible, then, to see clearly how pungent this humour is from its opening haemorrhoids; but it also appears biting to those who use it, and for this reason we take care not to use yellow bile by itself alone for any other disease or symptom. For the kykliskoi mentioned take little of the bile; and of the drugs compounded for sharpness of sight, some take hyena's bile, others that of the partridge or the cock or some other animal, and they contain honey mixed in and fennel juice or opobalsam. The bile of certain animals has been especially praised by physicians as at once sharpening the sight and dispersing the beginnings of suffusions, such as that of the fish they call kallionymos, and that of the hyena, of the sea scorpion, of the hen and of the partridge. Weakest is that of swine, to such a degree that it is not even intolerable to ulcers; it appears the most watery of all biles, except that of wild swine that live in the mountains. For just as their whole flesh is hotter and drier, so too is their bile. Some use the bile of domestic swine for ulcers in the ears, a drug not without repute, and you too should use it when no other of the compound drugs is available, for there are countless of them. According to the magnitude of the condition, the bile of some other animal could also be suitable. For when the ulcer is chronic and has much ichor and pus, it will tolerate the more drying biles as well, such as that of sheep, which is slightly more pungent than that of swine, and, more so than this, that of goats, to which that of bears and of oxen is somewhat similar. That of bulls is stronger than these, but falls short of that of hyenas. This in turn falls short of that of the kallionymos, the sea scorpion and the sea turtle. Some have written that the bile of the wild goat benefits those suffering from nyctalopia. The biles of winged animals are all more pungent and more drying than those in quadrupeds, and among the winged animals themselves those of hens and partridges are better for medical use. Those of hawks and eagles are markedly pungent and are also erosive; for this reason they also appear verdigris-like in colour, and sometimes even black. Knowing, then, these differences among them, and knowing also which affections need to be dried more and which less, if you have tested any one bile whatsoever by its effects, you will be able to pass from these to the others by method, so as always to employ the one that suits the affection. For since the intensity of each power lies in conjecture, you must pass from some defined starting-point to the untested material, having learned the degrees of excess among them from what has been tested beforehand. And I have also gone through for you clear signs taken from the colour of the biles and the mixture of the animals.

For this comprises the differences among the regions with respect to heat and cold, just as it does the seasons of the year and the present or the preceding state. Whenever, then, the account concerns urines or sweats or blood or fat or suet or any other of the things in the body, as we distinguish the differences among animals, one must understand the account as referring to healthy bodies, which are in the middle state of their own proper mixture. Human urine is almost the weakest of all the other urines, except that of domestic pigs whose testicles they cut out. Strong, on the other hand, is that of the boars in the mountains, as is evident from its smell too, which is most pungent. For tasting those urines is most loathsome, given that even the urine of boys a certain man notable in character and way of life could not bring himself to drink when he fell ill with the pestilential disease in Syria, during which many, having drunk urine, some of boys and some of men, were thought to have been saved by it. Human urine, then, is of cleansing power if anything else is, as many show, and the fullers among them, who clean out and wash off for us the dirty garments with it. Physicians too, having observed this power of it, scour off psora and lepra with it, and pour it over those ulcers that are full of much moisture, filth and impurity, and much more so when they have something putrefactive. They also inject urine into the private parts when these are so affected, and into ears that discharge pus. And they treat achores and pityra with it, pouring it over the head. raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.16] [16. On saliva.] Saliva: whether one wishes to call it sielon, or sialon, or ptyelon, makes no difference to me. One must know, however, that its power differs both among the kinds of animals and, within each of them, according as the animal is healthy or sick, has eaten or drunk, or is without drink and fasting. For as with urine, the biles and sweat, so too spittle is weak in those who have eaten, but strong and pungent in those who have been excessively thirsty and excessively hungry. Midway between the two is that of those who have digested well but have not yet eaten or drunk. Accordingly, it is with this saliva that children's nurses too cure leichenes: they wet the little finger and then rub the affected skin. They do this often, so that the power derived from the saliva is preserved in the leichen during the time between applications. Many country people, too, chew wheat grains and apply them to boils, for it disperses them and concocts them quickly. And yet if the grains were moistened with water, they would not help in the same way. It is quite clear, then, that the saliva itself supplies the strength of the benefit. On soft bodies and those of children, however, they apply not wheat but bread, which they have chewed. All things chewed in this way disperse both bruises and the other ecchymoses, and more so when the bread has been chewed together with a little radish. response.translation: [10.2.16] [16. On saliva.] Saliva: whether one wishes to call it sielon, or sialon, or ptyelon, makes no difference to me. One must know, however, that its power differs both among the kinds of animals and, within each of them, according as the animal is healthy or sick, has eaten or drunk, or is without drink and fasting. For as with urine, the biles and sweat, so too spittle is weak in those who have eaten, but strong and pungent in those who have been excessively thirsty and excessively hungry. Midway between the two is that of those who have digested well but have not yet eaten or drunk. Accordingly, it is with this saliva that children's nurses too cure leichenes: they wet the little finger and then rub the affected skin. They do this often, so that the power derived from the saliva is preserved in the leichen during the time between applications. Many country people, too, chew wheat grains and apply them to boils, for it disperses them and concocts them quickly. And yet if the grains were moistened with water, they would not help in the same way. It is quite clear, then, that the saliva itself supplies the strength of the benefit. On soft bodies and those of children, however, they apply not wheat but bread, which they have chewed. All things chewed in this way disperse both bruises and the other ecchymoses, and more so when the bread has been chewed together with a little radish. By its whole substance spittle is most contrary to the beasts that kill human beings, as Nicander the poet also says somewhere. Someone who had promised to show me an incantation that kills scorpions spoke it once and spat upon the scorpion; next he spoke it a second time and spat again; then, when he had spoken it a third time and spat down upon it, the scorpion died. Later I myself saw, without the incantation, the scorpion die from the saliva alone, and suffer this very thing quickly with the spittle of people who were hungry and thirsty, slowly with that of people filled with foods and drinks, and proportionally with that of the others.

response.translation: [10.2.19] [19. On dog's dung.] I myself, at any rate, know it, having experienced the wonderful power both of human dung and of dog's dung. I shall tell you first about the dog's, which one of our teachers used continually. He gave a dog nothing but bones to eat for two days in succession, as a result of which the dung becomes hard and white and least ill-smelling. Taking this, then, he dried it, so that later, whenever he wished to use it, it could easily be ground fine. He used it for synanchai, for dysenteries and for the most chronic of ulcers. For synanchai he mixed it with the drugs that are suited to this affection in any case. In the case of dysenteric patients he mixed it with boiled milk into which the so-called pebbles (kachlēkes), red-hot, had been thrown, or, as I later came to do with iron because it is easy to procure, throwing this red-hot into milk that had first been well boiled. Some of the physicians, I do not know why, call such milk 'split' (schiston). For this ought not to be called so; rather, the name belongs to the cases in which we separate and split the whey from the cheesy part. But the physician ground some dry dog's dung and threw it, without its being noticed, into the milk that had the pebbles quenched in it, and he taught this to his most genuine pupils alone. Of these two uses of dog's dung, then, I have a very great deal of experience, as of a wonderful drug, just as I have of its use for the most malignant ulcers. For in those cases too he mixed a little dog's dung with the approved drugs, and the drug clearly became stronger than it had been by itself. And wherever there was need to disperse and dry something, he mixed it into those drugs as well.

On goat's dung.] I have mentioned human, dog's and wolf's dung, but not yet the others, although several more still remain besides those already discussed, some of which have a very frequent use and others a rarer one. The dung we use most frequently is that of goats; these droppings are specifically called spyrathoi. They are of a pungent and dispersing power, so that they are suitable for indurated (scirrhous) swellings not only of the spleen, for which many physicians use such dung most frequently, but also of other parts. I myself used it on a knee that had a chronic swelling, hard to resolve: I ordered it to be applied as a poultice with oxycrate, barley meal being added to the dung, and the man was wonderfully benefited. The man on whom this was done was one of the rustics. Another rustic too has since been benefited in the same way, using it similarly for similar swellings, not only on the knee but also on other parts. For the drug is too pungent to treat town women or children, or soft-fleshed people in general. But the particular use of all drugs will be discussed in the work on their composition. We also use goat's dung in many ways in the case of the dropsical and the splenic. Moreover, when burnt it becomes more fine-particled, though not clearly more pungent. Hence it is suitable for alopeciai and for all the conditions that require cleansing drugs, such as leprai, psorai and leichenes, and the others of this kind. It is also mixed into dispersing poultices, such as those for parotids and for buboes that have become chronic. For its power, both unburnt and burnt, is cleansing and dispersing, and its dispersing quality is not slight. At any rate, a certain physician of those who practise in the fields and villages used it with vinegar against the bites of vipers, and still more against those of the other venomous beasts, and saved a great many. I myself used it on a knee that had a chronic swelling, hard to resolve: I ordered it to be applied as a poultice with oxycrate, barley meal being added to the dung, and the man was wonderfully benefited. The man on whom this was done was one of the rustics. Another rustic too has since been benefited in the same way, using it similarly for similar swellings, not only on the knee but also on other parts. For the drug is too pungent to treat town women or children, or soft-fleshed people in general. But the particular use of all drugs will be discussed in the work on their composition. We also use goat's dung in many ways in the case of the dropsical and the splenic. Moreover, when burnt it becomes more fine-particled, though not clearly more pungent. Hence it is suitable for alopeciai and for all the conditions that require cleansing drugs, such as leprai, psorai and leichenes, and the others of this kind. It is also mixed into dispersing poultices, such as those for parotids and for buboes that have become chronic. For its power, both unburnt and burnt, is cleansing and dispersing, and its dispersing quality is not slight. At any rate, a certain physician of those who practise in the fields and villages used it with vinegar against the bites of vipers, and still more against those of the other venomous beasts, and saved a great many. This same physician also gave spyrathoi in wine to the jaundiced to drink, and used them against female flux, applying them together with frankincense. The best physician must know all such things, but must select the better ones, especially in the case of town-dwelling and distinguished men, for whom I would never have used such a drug, having an abundance of very many better ones. Nevertheless the need for such things does sometimes arise on journeys, at hunts and during a stay in the country, when none of the better remedies is at hand, or when the person is a hard-fleshed rustic, like an ass. For many such people in the countryside are fit to drink spyrathoi. And what was said in the preceding sections about urines, biles and salivas, remember now too: the general and common power is the same in all kinds of dung, but it varies according to the mixtures of the animals. For the dung of animals drier in mixture is also more drying, just as that of hotter animals is more heating; but none cools, just as none moistens. There would also be a great difference arising from the nature of what they have eaten, and for this reason the difference is greater in humans than in the other animals, because this animal uses the most varied food. For what likeness is there between those who have eaten garlic and onions and those who have eaten gourd, if it so happened? The spyrathoi of a goat, by contrast, would differ a little from one another according to the pastures, but not nearly as much as human dung does.

raw_text: {"translation": "[10.2.30] [30. On the dirt of human beings.] Dirt is generated not only over the whole skin of the body but also in the ears. Because there is so little of it, however, it is hard to procure, and for this reason nothing has been written about it, except that the dirt from the ear is suitable for paronychiae; and this is the only kind that can be obtained by itself. For the dirt that accumulates on the whole skin is cleansed off in the baths and the palaestrae, and it too contributes something to what is called patos, which has been discussed earlier. Its generation also shows its nature. For if dirt comes to be as the coarse-particled and earthy residue of what is evacuated through imperceptible transpiration, it is of a drying power, and has something of heat as well. The dirt that accumulates on the fleeces of sheep, however, from which they make what is called oesypum, is of a concocting power, similar to butter; and it also has a slight dispersing [power]. response.translation: [10.2.30] [30. On the dirt of human beings.] Dirt is generated not only over the whole skin of the body but also in the ears. Because there is so little of it, however, it is hard to procure, and for this reason nothing has been written about it, except that the dirt from the ear is suitable for paronychiae; and this is the only kind that can be obtained by itself. For the dirt that accumulates on the whole skin is cleansed off in the baths and the palaestrae, and it too contributes something to what is called patos, which has been discussed earlier. Its generation also shows its nature. For if dirt comes to be as the coarse-particled and earthy residue of what is evacuated through imperceptible transpiration, it is of a drying power, and has something of heat as well. The dirt that accumulates on the fleeces of sheep, however, from which they make what is called oesypum, is of a concocting power, similar to butter; and it also has a slight dispersing [power]. raw_text: {"translation": "[9.1.2] [2. On the differences of what is customarily called earth.] I said that it is customary among all Greeks to call earth that which, when thrown into liquid, at once dissolves and becomes mud. These differences are the most opposed; the others lie between them, either approaching one of the two more than the other, while some even seem to be exactly in the middle, standing at an equal distance from both. Other differences of earth arise from the admixture of bodies of another kind, in so far as earths are stony and sandy. People separate the admixed substance from such earths by soaking them and kneading them up with much water until they make the whole liquid. For when this settles, everything of the stony and sandy kind that was borne along in it sinks to the bottom, and the pure earth floats on top. Something of this sort is done with the Lemnian earth, which some call Lemnian red ochre and certain others Lemnian seal, because of the seal sacred to Artemis that is impressed upon it. The priestess takes this earth with a certain local rite, in which no animals are sacrificed but wheat and barley are given to the place in return, and brings it to the city. She kneads it up with water, makes a liquid mud, and stirs this vigorously; then, having let it settle, she first removes the water on the surface. Next she takes the oily part of the earth beneath it, leaving behind only the stony and sandy sediment, which is also useless, and dries the oily mud until it reaches the consistency of soft wax. Taking small portions of this, she impresses on them the sacred seal of Artemis, and then dries them again in the shade until they are made completely free of moisture. So is produced the drug known to all physicians, the Lemnian seal. For, as I said, some call it so because of the seal impressed upon it, just as some, because of its colour, call it Lemnian red ochre. It has the same colour as red ochre, but differs from it in not staining when touched, as that does. And [it is found] on the hill in Lemnos which is entirely tawny in colour, on which there is neither tree nor rock nor plant, but only earth of this sort. Three differences of it are found: one is the aforementioned sacred earth, which no one touches except the priestess; the second is another, that of true red ochre, which carpenters use most of all; the third is that of the cleansing earth, which those who wash linens and garments use if they wish. Having read in Dioscorides and certain others that goat's blood is mixed with the Lemnian earth, and that from the mud produced by this mixture the priestess moulds and seals what they call Lemnian seals, I myself was eager to inquire into the proportion of the mixture. So, just as I travelled to Cyprus for the sake of its mines, and to Coele Syria, which is part of Palestine, for the sake of asphalt and certain other things there worth inquiring into, so too I did not hesitate to sail to Lemnos, to see how much of the blood is mixed with the earth. On the second occasion, when I was to reach Rome from Asia travelling on foot through Thrace and Macedonia, I first sailed from Alexandria Troas to Lemnos, having found a ship putting out for Thessalonica, the ship-master having agreed to put in at Lemnos first. He did put in, but not at the city where he should have. For I did not even know at first that there were two cities on the island; I supposed that Lemnos, like Samos, Chios, Cos, Andros, Tenos and all the islands of the Aegean, had a single city bearing the same name as the whole island. When I left the ship, I learned that the city was called Myrina, and that neither the place associated with Philoctetes nor the hill sacred to Hephaestus lay in the territory of that city, but in that of the other, called Hephaestias, and that that city was not even near Myrina. As the ship-master could not wait for me, I put off seeing Hephaestias until another time, when I should come from Rome to Asia. And this was accomplished for me just as I had hoped and intended. For when I had crossed from Italy into Macedonia and, having travelled through almost the whole of it on foot, arrived at Philippi, which is a city bordering on Thrace, I went down from there to the nearby sea, a hundred and twenty stades distant, and sailed first to Thasos, about two hundred stades, and from there to Lemnos, seven hundred, and then again from Lemnos the same seven hundred to Alexandria Troas. I have written about the voyage and the stades on purpose, so that if anyone wishes, like me, to see Hephaestias for himself, he may know its position and prepare himself accordingly for the voyage. For on the whole island of Lemnos, Hephaestias lies in the part towards the east, and Myrina in the part towards the west. And as for what the poet says of Hephaestus, 'he fell in Lemnos', the myth seems to me to rest on the nature of the hill. For it appears very like something burnt, both in its colour and because nothing grows on it. To this hill, then, the priestess came at the very time when I landed on the island; she cast a certain number of wheat and barley grains onto the earth, performed certain other things according to the local worship, and filled a whole wagon with the earth. Having brought it to the city, she prepared, as I said just now, the much-celebrated Lemnian seals. It seemed good to me, then, to inquire whether they had received any account of he-goat's or goat's blood having ever formerly been mixed with this earth. At this question all who heard it laughed, and they were not ordinary men, but very well educated, both in other matters and in the whole local history. Indeed I also received a book from one of them, written formerly by one of the local men, in which he taught the entire use of the Lemnian earth; whence I too did not hesitate to make trial of the drug, taking twenty thousand seals. The man who gave me the book, who was counted among the foremost of Hephaestias, himself used the drug for many purposes. He used the seal for wounds, both old and hard to cicatrise, for viper bites and bites of venomous animals generally, and for deadly drugs, not only giving it beforehand but also afterwards. He said too that he had experience of the drug made with juniper berries, into which the Lemnian earth is also put, which provokes vomiting if someone drinks the remedy against it while the deadly drug is still in the belly. We ourselves have experience of this in the case of the sea-hare and cantharides: persons who suspected that they had taken something of the sort vomited everything at once on taking the drug made with the Lemnian seal, and afterwards suffered none of the symptoms that follow the sea-hare and cantharides, although the administration of the deadly drugs had been established. Whether the drug made with juniper berries and the Lemnian earth has the same power against the other deadly drugs too, those called poisons, is unclear to me. But the man from Hephaestias went so far as to declare that it heals even the bite of a rabid dog, when drunk in diluted wine and applied to the ulcer in very pungent vinegar. He said also that in vinegar it heals the bites of the other venomous animals, with the leaves of herbs laid on externally, herbs which we have learnt act contrary to putrefactions; he praised most of all skordion, then the slender centaury, then prasion. Moreover, whenever I used the Lemnian earth on malignant and putrefactive ulcers, it helped greatly. The use is made according to the degree of the ulcer's badness. For the foul-smelling, very flabby and dirty ulcer tolerates the Lemnian earth dissolved in the most pungent vinegar to a muddy consistency, in the same way as the troches, of which different people use different ones, I mean those of Polyeidus, Pasion and Andron, and this one now mentioned, which is called the Betinus. For all these, drying strongly, benefit malignant ulcers, being diluted sometimes with sweet wine, sometimes with siraion, sometimes with honeyed wine [oinomeli], sometimes with some of the white wines or the tawny or yellow ones, as need requires; for these matters will be determined elsewhere. Likewise they are sometimes diluted with vinegar, and with wine or water or oxymel, or oxycrate and melikraton. And the Lemnian earth too, diluted with each of the substances mentioned, is a drug suited both to the agglutination of fresh wounds and to the healing of chronic, hard-to-cicatrise or malignant ones. response.translation: [9.1.3] [3. On the washing of earth.] Every earth is washed in the same manner as was stated before concerning the Lemnian. First it is kneaded up with water that shows no trace of any medicinal quality. Then, when the mud has settled and the water has been removed from the top, the [layer] beneath it is next separated from the stony and sandy matter that settles to the bottom. And if you also have a trained gustatory sense, you will yourself be an exact judge of which earth must be washed and which not. For some do not need washing, while others need to be washed twice or three times. The Lemnian, then, you receive ready, washed once already by the priestess, and not needing to be washed a second time.

As a result, some of those who had such ulcers seemed to be completely rid of them. Of those who travelled from Rome to Libya for this reason, some were fully convinced that they were healthy and lived without complaint for some years. Then at some later time, when they lived more carelessly, a relapse of the disease occurred. These people, as I said, the Armenian clod (bōlos) plainly helped, even though they were living in Rome, and it helped still more those continually short of breath. In this great plague, similar in form to the one that occurred in Thucydides' time, all who drank this drug were quickly cured. All whom it did not help died, nor were they helped by anything else, which also makes it clear that it failed to help only those who were incurable. It is drunk with wine of thin consistency, mixed moderately if the person is entirely without fever or only slightly feverish, but very watery if he is more feverish. Plague fevers, however, are not vehement in their heat. As for ulcers that need drying, what need is there even to say how great a power this Armenian clod has? As I said, you may call it a stone, as the man who gave it named it, or an earth, as I would say, since it is soaked by liquids.

response.translation: [9.2.3] [3. On schistos and many other stones.] A power similar to that of this stone, but weaker, is possessed by the stone called schistos, and after it by galaktites. Melitites, as I said, has already taken on something of heat as well. Each of them, then, departing little by little from the power of haematites, is likewise brought into use for the eyes, but is milder. Milder drugs are always gentler for parts that are still inflamed, but weaker for bringing to complete health parts that have ceased to be inflamed. Drying is common to all stones. Those of them which, whether dissolved into a juice or pounded fine in some other way, have at first no quality perceptible to the taste must be considered the weakest, the gentlest and the least biting. Those which appear to display some clear quality to the taste have a strength proportionate to that quality. If they are astringent, their strength is for repressing, constricting, compacting and drawing together. If they are biting, it is for heating, dispersing and melting. Intermediate between them are those that are only cleansing, without being astringent or biting. Now haematites and schistos, galaktites and melitites dissolve into a juice when rubbed, as I said, on whetstones and in mortars. There are also other stones that dissolve into a juice, such as the one produced in Egypt, which people use to glaze linen cloths. This stone is more devoid of quality than those already mentioned, displaying neither astringency nor cleansing nor biting. Hence this very thing alone belongs to this stone, namely drying. For this reason they mix it with cerate and use it for the cicatrization of ulcers in soft bodies. Such stones are also mixed into ophthalmic preparations, in the same way as those mentioned before. By as much as it is more softening than they are, through having no active quality, by so much it is more moderate and produces less sensation. Some people call this stone moroxos, others graphis.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.1] On metallic drugs. [1. On the general accounts, concretions and powers of metals.] It is customary among physicians to call 'metallic drugs' those whose generation takes place in the mines, whether it is self-grown or comes about by means of a furnace. And third, in addition to these, are all those that people in turn prepare from these very things in whatever manner, such as white lead (psimmythion), psorikon, sandyx and phykos. Next, then, all of them will be discussed in the order of the letters with which each of their names begins, once we have first said in advance something common to all of them, as we did a little before in the case of the stones, and, earlier than these, concerning medicinal earth. For just as those, so in the same way all metallic drugs too have drying in common. For their substance is earthy, as I am now using the name in the sense of the elemental earth. But just as storage jars, roof-tiles, cooking-pots and the other things of this kind are made by us from potter's earth, being hardened by fire once its moisture has been roasted out, in the same way, in the earth, when a long-lasting warmth unites and blends the substance mixed from earth and water, and sometimes also air, and then dries it, the concretions of the metallic drugs come into being. And the nature of the places in which these concrete, according as they are more or less cold, congeals some more and others less.
