response.translation: [9.3.1] On metallic drugs. [1. On the general accounts, concretions and powers of metals.] It is customary among physicians to call 'metallic drugs' those whose generation takes place in the mines, whether it is self-grown or comes about by means of a furnace. And third, in addition to these, are all those that people in turn prepare from these very things in whatever manner, such as white lead (psimmythion), psorikon, sandyx and phykos. Next, then, all of them will be discussed in the order of the letters with which each of their names begins, once we have first said in advance something common to all of them, as we did a little before in the case of the stones, and, earlier than these, concerning medicinal earth. For just as those, so in the same way all metallic drugs too have drying in common. For their substance is earthy, as I am now using the name in the sense of the elemental earth. But just as storage jars, roof-tiles, cooking-pots and the other things of this kind are made by us from potter's earth, being hardened by fire once its moisture has been roasted out, in the same way, in the earth, when a long-lasting warmth unites and blends the substance mixed from earth and water, and sometimes also air, and then dries it, the concretions of the metallic drugs come into being. And the nature of the places in which these concrete, according as they are more or less cold, congeals some more and others less. Just as, then, in the varieties of earth the substance of the elemental earth is very great and that of the airy is small, so in mined substances much of the fiery has been mixed in. Between them are the stones; and for this reason most of the metallic drugs, when washed, some once or twice, others more often, become useful for powers that dry without biting. Such, then, are the general accounts which it is necessary to know beforehand about all of them; next will be stated the account proper to each, in the order of the letters with which the names of the drugs begin.

[9.3.2] [2. On salts.] Salts. Some of these too come from the sea, in the so-called salt-pans, which we shall also mention among the marine drugs. But there are also the so-called dug salts, which are included in the class of the metallic drugs. All of them, both the dug ones and those from the sea, have a power similar to one another. They were discussed earlier, in the fourth book, in the account where we distinguished the salty and briny flavour from the bitter. It will be said now as well that the flavour in aphronitre is bitter and cleansing, while that in salts falls as far short in cleansing as it exceeds in astringency. For it is mixed from two qualities, a cleansing and an astringent one. That both of them dry considerably had also been shown before. In the middle between both is the flavour of litron.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.10] [10. On verdigris.] Verdigris has a pungent quality to those who taste it, and it is dispersing, reducing and colliquative not only of soft but also of hard flesh. It was said in what went before that some people call many drugs of this kind scarring, because, having ground it fine and made it downy, they touch ulcers with overgrown flesh with the bulb of a probe. response.translation: [9.3.14] [14. On lye made from ash.] Lye. Lye comes into being when ash has been washed; and the Greeks call 'ash' the residue of burnt bodies, whether these be stony in nature or parts of trees or of animals. The lye, then, also comes to be according to the nature of what is washed: from that which has a most pungent fiery quality acquired in burning, it is most pungent; from that which is not of this kind, it is more moderate. For this reason it is also mixed into the so-called putrefying preparations, since it has a caustic heat, burning painlessly through the fine-particled character of its substance.

In its right-hand wall (left, as regards us who were entering) there was an entrance into the mine itself, in which I saw three bands, as it were, extending over a very great length one upon another: the lowest that of sory, upon it that of chalcitis, then that of misy. The overseer of the mine at that time, showing me these, said: \"Just as you have come now when we are in poverty of the cadmia that is smelted in furnaces, so you see these three established in wonderful abundance.\" And accordingly I took a very great quantity of it and carried it first to Asia, and from there to Rome, and I have kept it until now, about thirty years having passed in between. And by a certain chance the present treatise advanced as far as the eighth book, about twenty years ago, without this ninth one being added to it, because I had not yet seen some of the stones, and moreover also because of the occupations that intervened on account of other matters. But now, as I was adding this ninth book, there occurred in the meantime by chance a most beautiful sight, such as one might have contrived on purpose oneself. For, needing misy for a certain drug that was being prepared, I took up a lump about a handful in size, although misy does not at all usually have such a consistency, but breaks up into small aggregates. Wondering, then, at its unaccustomed compactness, I crushed the lump and found misy on the surface all round, like a kind of efflorescence of what was inside; and next to it, between chalcitis and misy, a sort of half-way change, as it were, from chalcitis into misy. In its right-hand wall (left, as regards us who were entering) there was an entrance into the mine itself, in which I saw three bands, as it were, extending over a very great length one upon another: the lowest that of sory, upon it that of chalcitis, then that of misy. The overseer of the mine at that time, showing me these, said: "Just as you have come now when we are in poverty of the cadmia that is smelted in furnaces, so you see these three established in wonderful abundance." And accordingly I took a very great quantity of it and carried it first to Asia, and from there to Rome, and I have kept it until now, about thirty years having passed in between. And by a certain chance the present treatise advanced as far as the eighth book, about twenty years ago, without this ninth one being added to it, because I had not yet seen some of the stones, and moreover also because of the occupations that intervened on account of other matters. But now, as I was adding this ninth book, there occurred in the meantime by chance a most beautiful sight, such as one might have contrived on purpose oneself. For, needing misy for a certain drug that was being prepared, I took up a lump about a handful in size, although misy does not at all usually have such a consistency, but breaks up into small aggregates. Wondering, then, at its unaccustomed compactness, I crushed the lump and found misy on the surface all round, like a kind of efflorescence of what was inside; and next to it, between chalcitis and misy, a sort of half-way change, as it were, from chalcitis into misy. For the lump had originally been a lump of chalcitis. And as much of it as lay in the depth was pure chalcitis, having as yet undergone no alteration. Having seen this, and having reflected that in the mine too misy is generated upon chalcitis in this way, just as verdigris is upon copper, I examined the sory that is still preserved in my possession, to see whether it was undergoing any change into chalcitis; and a slight indication appeared, which perhaps would itself also be able in a long time to undergo the change into chalcitis. So it is nothing surprising that the three drugs, I mean sory, chalcitis and misy, are of a homogeneous power, differing in fineness of particles and coarseness of particles. For the most coarse-particled among them is sory, the most fine-particled is misy, and chalcitis has a power intermediate between the two. All three burn and produce what are called eschars; yet, although they burn, they do share in astringency. Misy, when applied to hard flesh, is less biting than chalcitis, although it is not less hot than it; it has this from the fine-particled character of its substance. And whereas both are fusible in boilings, chalcitis more so than misy, sory does not melt, because it has a more stony and more vehement solidification; just as, again, misy, from having been worked upon by its innate heat, being drier than chalcitis, is reasonably also harder to melt.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.23] [23. On lead.] Lead is of a cooling power. For it has not only much moist substance congealed by cold, but also airy substance, while it partakes of little earthy substance. That it has a very great amount of moist substance congealed by cold, let the melting and flowing that comes about in it quickly whenever it meets fire be your proof. That it also has airy substance, this is a sign: lead alone (μόνος μόνος, sic) of the things we know increases both in bulk and in weight when it is stored in underground chambers that have turbid air, such that the things lying in them are quickly filled with mould; and the leads that bind the feet of statues to their stones have often been seen to have grown. Some have even risen to so great a bulk that they hang down from the stones like ice. These, then, are plausible indications, prior to experience, of its moistness and coldness. But what is scientific and secure is known through experience. If, then, having prepared a mortar of lead, you put into it, together with a pestle of lead, whatever liquid you wish, and grind it so that the pestle and the lead give off some juice, you will find that what is produced from both is far colder in power than the liquid was. You may put in water, thin watery wine, oil and anything at all of that kind. If you wish to make the juice still more refrigerant, let the oil be omphacine oil, rose oil, quince oil or myrtle oil. Using the juice so produced for inflammations arising in the seat with ulcers or folds, and for those in the genitals, testicles and breasts, you will have an excellent drug. Likewise also against all the other fluxes when they are beginning, such as settle into buboes, the feet or the other joints, and moreover also for malignant ulcers, so that, using it for cancerous ones too, you will marvel at the drug. If you wish to collect a great deal of the juice of lead quickly, try grinding in the sun or in air that has become warm in any way whatever. raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.33] [33. On phykos.] What power phykos has will be stated in the discussion of white lead. [9.3.34] [34. On chalcanthum.] Chalcanthum. I have also made an inquiry concerning chalcanthum, which by chance was changing into chalcitis. For I brought this drug too from Cyprus in great quantity. All of its outer part, after about twenty years, became chalcitis, while what was inside was still chalcanthum. For this reason I still keep, even now, what is changing in this way, watching whether the change advances into the depth each year, as with the change of chalcitis into misy, as has been said before. One may wonder at how, in this drug, a not ignoble heat is mixed with a most powerful astringency. It is clear, then, that it is able beyond all others to pickle moist flesh, consuming the moisture by its heat and, by its astringency, drawing together and compacting the substance. For in this action it squeezes out besides some of the moisture itself, and it binds, dries and draws together towards itself the substance of the whole flesh. Now in Cyprus, at the time when I was there, I saw this drug being collected in the following manner. There was a building, large but not high, lying in front of the entrance to the mine. And in the left wall of this building, which was on the right hand for those entering, a passage had been hewn out into the adjoining hill, in breadth such that three men would touch one another, in height such that the tallest man could walk upright. This passage sloped downward, though not steeply or precipitously. At its end, the passage being about a stade long, there was a pit full of green, thick, lukewarm water. Throughout the whole descent there was a warmth similar to that in the first rooms of the baths, which they are accustomed to call promalaktēria. The water collected each day amounted to about eight Roman amphorae, coming down in small drops over the twenty-four hours of the whole day and night from the bored-through hill. Certain fettered convicts carried this water up and poured it into square tubs in the building in front, made of earthenware, in which, solidifying in a few days, it became chalcanthum. When I went down to the end of the excavation, where the lukewarm and green water collected, the odour of the air appeared to me stifling and hard to bear, smelling of chalcitis and of verdigris. The water itself, when tasted, also had such a quality. For this reason the fettered convicts carried up the amphorae naked and in haste, and did not endure to linger longer, but ran quickly back up, lamps burning on either side in the walls of the excavation at moderate intervals; and these themselves did not last a long time either, but went out very quickly. I heard from them that this excavation had been dug little by little over many years. response.translation: [9.3.38] [38. On chrysocolla.] Chrysocolla. This drug too is among those that melt down flesh; it does not, however, bite strongly, but it is sufficiently dispersing and drying. Now some people give this name only to the mined kind, while others give it to the kind prepared in a copper mortar with a copper pestle by means of a boy's urine, which some count among the varieties of verdigris. This drug is most suitable for malignant ulcers, both on its own and mixed with others, as will be said in the works on the composition of drugs. response.translation: [9.3.39] [39. On white lead.] White lead (psimmythion). This drug too bears witness to the power stated just before this one. At any rate, although it comes from being dissolved by pungent vinegar, when tasted it is nevertheless neither pungent nor biting nor dispersing, but clogging and cooling, being of a power most contrary to verdigris (ios). And yet verdigris too comes about when vinegar dissolves copper. White lead, when burnt, changing into what is called sandyx, becomes a drug more fine-particled than itself, but not yet, at any rate, heating. Phykos, however, preserving the cooling quality of white lead, has taken on fineness of particles, so that through it its power is able to sink down into the depth of the bodies with which it comes into contact.

raw_text: {"translation": "[9.3.40] [40. On psoricum.] Psoricum. The drug is made from litharge mixed with twice as much chalcitis. Both are first ground in the most pungent vinegar and then put into a new pot, which you will bury in dung for forty days in midsummer. This drug becomes both more drying and at the same time less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10. None of the things now about to be said will bring great benefit to those who are ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books. Perhaps it will even harm a person who uses the drugs written about in it without having a method. I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, after recalling the main point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs act according to the so-called active qualities, heat and coldness and dryness and moisture. Through the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and briny and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet. Some become cleansing, others repelling, others drawing, others softening, others caustic, others putrefying, others eschar-forming. In addition to these, according to other more specific actions, they become flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh. It was also shown that the universal power would be discovered indicatively from a single trial. This is not just any trial, but one carried out with the distinctions that were stated. Once the universal power has been discovered, there is no longer any need of trial for the particular actions, except solely for confirmation of what reason has discovered. In this way, then, let us now too make our judgement of the material before us, and this is the material from animals. For in the three books that follow the fifth in sequence, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants. We did not, evidently, go through all of it throughout the whole inhabited world, but only as much as we have experience of. In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, we went through the material concerning earthy and stony bodies. It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals. After that there still remains what is generated in the sea and lakes, or generally in water, things which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are altogether very few, and they will be written of last, after we have gone through what concerns the bodies of animals. The order of instruction for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names. In the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices that come from them. So now too the instruction about power will concern not only the solid parts in animals but also what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. In what was said earlier, not many of the particular items in the materia medica written by the physicians remained unknown to me. I myself took pains to know their powers through experience. If there was something I did not know, I did not write about it at all, since I did not think it right to trust others about even one such thing, because I had learned that some people tell many lies. With the material now before us, however, it is not so. I confess that there are very many of the parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written about. For some of them are licentious and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws. About these I do not know how Xenocrates came to write. He was a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden men to eat human beings. Yet he, at any rate, writes quite credibly, as one who had himself made trial of them. He records which affections the brain or flesh or liver of a human being naturally cures when eaten, and which the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure when drunk, some burnt and others unburnt, and which blood itself cures. These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not licentious. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menses is licentious and disgusting. No less so than these is dung. Xenocrates wrote what it can do when smeared on the parts in the mouth and pharynx and when swallowed into the stomach. He has also written about ear-wax when swallowed. I, for my part, would not have consented to swallow even this, even on condition of never falling ill. And I consider dung far more disgusting than it. Indeed, it is a greater reproach for a temperate man to be called a dung-eater than a doer of obscene acts or a catamite. But even among those who do obscene acts we loathe the 'phoenicizers' more than the 'lesbianizers', and the one who drinks menses seems to me to suffer something similar to the former. No man in his natural condition, then, would consent to make trial of these things. Nor would he consent to make trial of those that are more moderate than these but still licentious, such as smearing some part of the body with dung for the sake of the affection in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call it 'gonos'. He distinguishes with all care which conditions the gonos itself, by itself, naturally benefits when smeared on, and which it benefits after the intercourse of man and woman, when it falls out of the female bosom. For there must be some great poverty of remedies for anyone to treat chilblains [ὑπερεχούσας?] with a man's semen that has not stayed inside but has flowed out of the woman after intercourse. This kind of material too is plentiful in what he has written about the benefit from animals. For he recounts not only, evidently, for man, what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and when smeared on the parts in the mouth. He recounts this also for each of the other animals, and much else that is hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse. The beast called the basilisk I have never even seen, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Certain others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, and from them Xenocrates himself copied out most of what he wrote. For whence would he have had the means to make trial himself of so many and such things? Our own former king Attalus, at any rate, appears to write of fewer, although he was most ambitious in the testing of such things. Someone who praised the treatise of Ateuristus on the same subject also gave it to me to go through. As it seems to me, it had been composed without any personal autopsy on the part of the man who wrote it. I, then, shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses, nor anything else of which I myself have no experience. As for the so-called philtres, attraction-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms, I deliberately use their own very names for them. I would not have mentioned these in writing at all, not even if I had sufficient experience of them. In the same way I do not mention the deadly drugs, or those which they themselves call 'affection-producing'. Some of these are even ridiculous, such as binding one's legal opponents so that they cannot utter anything in court, or causing a pregnant woman to miscarry, or making her never conceive, and other such things. Most of these are, even by the test of experience, impossible. Some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men, so that I, by the gods, wonder with what intention certain people came to write them. Things that bring disrepute even to the living once they are known, how did they hope these would bring them good repute after death? Now if they had been kings and had made trial of these things on men condemned to death, they would have done nothing terrible. But they were private persons who had no such authority in their whole life, and yet they came to write these things. So it is one of two things. Either they write, without having made trial themselves, about what they do not know. Or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given deadly drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. Someone, at any rate, saw two physicians standing by the dealers in petty wares and brought them honey, supposedly to sell it. They tasted it and discussed the price, and as they offered little, he hurriedly went off [ἐχωρήθη], and neither of the physicians survived. All such things, then, deserve to be hated in those who wrote them no less than in those who did them, indeed even more. response.translation: [9.3.40] [40. On psoricum.] Psoricum. The drug is made from litharge mixed with twice as much chalcitis. Both are first ground in the most pungent vinegar and then put into a new pot, which you will bury in dung for forty days in midsummer. This drug becomes both more drying and at the same time less biting than chalcitis, and evidently also more fine-particled. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK 10. None of the things now about to be said will bring great benefit to those who are ignorant of what was said at the beginning of the treatise in the first five books. Perhaps it will even harm a person who uses the drugs written about in it without having a method. I shall therefore address you as one who has learned those things, after recalling the main point of the whole treatise. It was shown that drugs act according to the so-called active qualities, heat and coldness and dryness and moisture. Through the mixture of these they become acerbic and harsh and briny and salty and bitter and pungent and sweet. Some become cleansing, others repelling, others drawing, others softening, others caustic, others putrefying, others eschar-forming. In addition to these, according to other more specific actions, they become flesh-forming and cicatrizing and agglutinating of fistulas or ulcers, or reducing of overgrowing flesh. It was also shown that the universal power would be discovered indicatively from a single trial. This is not just any trial, but one carried out with the distinctions that were stated. Once the universal power has been discovered, there is no longer any need of trial for the particular actions, except solely for confirmation of what reason has discovered. In this way, then, let us now too make our judgement of the material before us, and this is the material from animals. For in the three books that follow the fifth in sequence, the sixth, seventh and eighth, we went through the material concerning plants. We did not, evidently, go through all of it throughout the whole inhabited world, but only as much as we have experience of. In the book before this one, the ninth of the whole treatise, we went through the material concerning earthy and stony bodies. It remains for us still to go through the material concerning animals. After that there still remains what is generated in the sea and lakes, or generally in water, things which are neither plants nor earth nor stone nor animal. Such things are altogether very few, and they will be written of last, after we have gone through what concerns the bodies of animals. The order of instruction for these too will follow the order of the first letters in their names. In the material of plants I also gave an account of the juices that come from them. So now too the instruction about power will concern not only the solid parts in animals but also what is contained in them: phlegm, bile, blood, urine, dung and the like. In what was said earlier, not many of the particular items in the materia medica written by the physicians remained unknown to me. I myself took pains to know their powers through experience. If there was something I did not know, I did not write about it at all, since I did not think it right to trust others about even one such thing, because I had learned that some people tell many lies. With the material now before us, however, it is not so. I confess that there are very many of the parts and fluids contained in the bodies of animals of which I myself have had no such experience as some have written about. For some of them are licentious and disgusting, and some are even forbidden by the laws. About these I do not know how Xenocrates came to write. He was a man who lived not long ago but in the time of our grandfathers, when the Roman empire had forbidden men to eat human beings. Yet he, at any rate, writes quite credibly, as one who had himself made trial of them. He records which affections the brain or flesh or liver of a human being naturally cures when eaten, and which the bones of the head or shin or fingers cure when drunk, some burnt and others unburnt, and which blood itself cures. These things, then, even if contrary to the laws, are at least not licentious. But the drinking of sweat and urine and a woman's menses is licentious and disgusting. No less so than these is dung. Xenocrates wrote what it can do when smeared on the parts in the mouth and pharynx and when swallowed into the stomach. He has also written about ear-wax when swallowed. I, for my part, would not have consented to swallow even this, even on condition of never falling ill. And I consider dung far more disgusting than it. Indeed, it is a greater reproach for a temperate man to be called a dung-eater than a doer of obscene acts or a catamite. But even among those who do obscene acts we loathe the 'phoenicizers' more than the 'lesbianizers', and the one who drinks menses seems to me to suffer something similar to the former. No man in his natural condition, then, would consent to make trial of these things. Nor would he consent to make trial of those that are more moderate than these but still licentious, such as smearing some part of the body with dung for the sake of the affection in it, or with human semen. Xenocrates is accustomed to call it 'gonos'. He distinguishes with all care which conditions the gonos itself, by itself, naturally benefits when smeared on, and which it benefits after the intercourse of man and woman, when it falls out of the female bosom. For there must be some great poverty of remedies for anyone to treat chilblains [ὑπερεχούσας?] with a man's semen that has not stayed inside but has flowed out of the woman after intercourse. This kind of material too is plentiful in what he has written about the benefit from animals. For he recounts not only, evidently, for man, what power urine has when drunk, or dung when swallowed and when smeared on the parts in the mouth. He recounts this also for each of the other animals, and much else that is hard to procure, as when he mentions the elephant or the Nile horse. The beast called the basilisk I have never even seen, and if what is said about it is true, it is dangerous even to come near this animal. Certain others too wrote things similar to Xenocrates about animals, and from them Xenocrates himself copied out most of what he wrote. For whence would he have had the means to make trial himself of so many and such things? Our own former king Attalus, at any rate, appears to write of fewer, although he was most ambitious in the testing of such things. Someone who praised the treatise of Ateuristus on the same subject also gave it to me to go through. As it seems to me, it had been composed without any personal autopsy on the part of the man who wrote it. I, then, shall mention neither basilisks nor elephants nor Nile horses, nor anything else of which I myself have no experience. As for the so-called philtres, attraction-charms, dream-senders and hate-charms, I deliberately use their own very names for them. I would not have mentioned these in writing at all, not even if I had sufficient experience of them. In the same way I do not mention the deadly drugs, or those which they themselves call 'affection-producing'. Some of these are even ridiculous, such as binding one's legal opponents so that they cannot utter anything in court, or causing a pregnant woman to miscarry, or making her never conceive, and other such things. Most of these are, even by the test of experience, impossible. Some, even if possible, are at any rate harmful to the life of men, so that I, by the gods, wonder with what intention certain people came to write them. Things that bring disrepute even to the living once they are known, how did they hope these would bring them good repute after death? Now if they had been kings and had made trial of these things on men condemned to death, they would have done nothing terrible. But they were private persons who had no such authority in their whole life, and yet they came to write these things. So it is one of two things. Either they write, without having made trial themselves, about what they do not know. Or, if they did make trial, they are the most impious of all men, having given deadly drugs for the sake of trial to those who had done no wrong, and sometimes even to fine and good men. Someone, at any rate, saw two physicians standing by the dealers in petty wares and brought them honey, supposedly to sell it. They tasted it and discussed the price, and as they offered little, he hurriedly went off [ἐχωρήθη], and neither of the physicians survived. All such things, then, deserve to be hated in those who wrote them no less than in those who did them, indeed even more. For it is a lesser wrong to do some evil alone than to do it along with many [ὅσῳ ... μετὰ πολλῶν]. The experience of evil precepts died together with the one who did the deed. But the experience of all those who wrote is immortal, furnishing the wicked with weapons of malefaction. Let us, then, now speak about the things useful to men, of which we have experience.

raw_text: {"translation": "[8.16.39] [39. On fern and female fern.] Fern has a root that is especially useful. For it kills the broad worm, if one takes a weight of four drachms of it in honey-water. [8.17.3] [3. On rhēon.] Rhēon, which some call rha, is of a mixed mixture and power. For it has something earthy and cold, as its astringency shows; but a certain heat is also present in it, for when chewed for a longer time it appears somewhat pungent. And indeed, that it partakes of a fine-particled, airy substance is shown both by its loose texture and its lightness, but not least also by its effects. For precisely because of this, although it is astringent, it nevertheless benefits not only strains (spasmata) but also ruptures and orthopnoea. So too it heals livid marks and leichenes when smeared on with vinegar. That the effects of its astringency are also vigorous may be learned from the benefit it gives to those who spit blood, to coeliacs and to dysenterics. For the fine-particled airy part does not work against the earthy cold part; rather, what guides it on its way and leads it into the depth becomes the cause of a stronger action.

For it has in itself on the one hand something earthy, and on the other something as it were sooty or fuliginous, or however one may wish to call it. These parts, then, are fine-particled, and when the ash is wetted with water and strained they are carried off along with it. Most people think that all things burnt become colder than they themselves were. Some, conversely, think that the heat of all burnt things is increased. Both err. For some will plainly appear to become hotter, in taste and touch and in the power observed in use, as I said earlier in the case of the pungent and the astringent things. Others, conversely, appear less hot after being burnt; and this we discern clearly both by sense and by use. By use I mean, as I said in the earlier cases, when, applied to the skin, some make it redder and hotter, others bloodless and cold, and some raise it into a swelling, while others contract it. The pungents, then, lose much of their heat when burnt, while those that are not such gain heat; but nothing burnt is completely cold. For there is left in them, as it were, a certain empyreuma (for Aristotle called it so), and this is what is washed away in washings. It is the most fine-particled part of the substance of burnt things. When it has gone off together with the water, the rest of the burnt thing is earthy substance. For burning consumes all the moisture, and what remains is earthy, together with what Aristotle called empyreuma. When, then, someone removes this and separates it by washing, the water in which the drug was washed has acquired a hot, fine-particled power, while the remainder becomes earthy and cold, able to dry without biting. I have spoken about these matters before as well, but it is no worse to recall them now too, so that someone who has the recollection of them fresh may follow more precisely what will be said.

raw_text: {"translation": "[7.10.19] [19. On the cherry.] The cherry tree bears a fruit that does not have an equal share of astringency in all the individual plants. For in these too, as also in pomegranates and apples, in some the harsh quality prevails, in some the sweet, and in some the sour. raw_text: {"translation": "[7.10.43] [43. On coriander.] Coriander (koriannon), or korion, or however you wish to name it: for the ancient Greeks call it koriannon, while the more recent physicians all name it korion, as does Dioscorides, who says, incorrectly, that the herb is cooling. For it is composed of contrary powers. It has much bitter substance, which was shown to be fine-particled and earthy, and not a little watery moisture, lukewarm in power, and it also has something of a slight astringency. From all of these it brings about, in varied ways, the effects that Dioscorides wrote of, but certainly not by cooling alone. But I shall set out the cause of each of its particular actions, even though my intention in the present account was to go through my own judgement only. Perhaps, though, nothing will prevent this; rather, if one must speak the truth, what is said in this manner about a few drugs will be of some benefit and will serve as a reminder of the methods set out earlier. First, then, not Dioscorides alone but also many other physicians make pronouncements about diseases without drawing distinctions, just as, indeed, even among present-day physicians one can find not a few who are well regarded in other respects but who err very greatly in this. For sometimes, when the part that has had the erysipelas has become black, livid and cold, and no longer needs cooling drugs as before, but now needs those that evacuate the humour unnaturally impacted in the region, these people still cool it. At other times they pass on to dispersing drugs, yet they say that they are curing erysipelas. And indeed they also prescribe some drugs while the cases of erysipelas are still beginning and increasing, and others when they are declining. But this is not how things are. For neither should it still be called erysipelas once its fiery, seething and bilious character has gone, nor should the remedies for such conditions be thought cold in their powers. Suppose that right at the start, whether from a blow or in any other way, a livid or black swelling had arisen in some part: it would have been thought to be a cold affection and to need dispersing and heating drugs. In the same way, if a hot condition should at some point change into a cold one, it is right to forget the former and to name the second by another name. Or, if you would not wish to change the name, but, as some do, write some remedies for the beginning and others for the decline, then at least you should not think that the drugs of the decline are also cold. One must grant that someone may call such a condition erysipelas if he wishes, but one must not grant that he still call it hot, once it has been chilled. Let us therefore not think either that what helps it at that time is cooling, as Dioscorides thinks coriander is, because, as he himself says, when applied as a poultice with bread or barley-groats it cures erysipelas. For an exact erysipelas, which is fiery and yellow, coriander with bread would never cure; it cures only one that is already cooling off. For this reason, in the earlier books, when we required that the power of each drug be tested by qualified experience, we advised choosing an affection as simple as possible. But most physicians do not know even that most diseases attack as compound right from the beginning. Nor do they know that exact erysipelas is one affection, and that which is now customarily called by all of us, or at any rate by the ancients, phlegmone is another. In between there are very many others: some one might call phlegmonous cases of erysipelas, others, as it were, certain erysipelatous phlegmonai. You may sometimes also find neither prevailing, but the two exactly balanced. Indeed, erysipelas sometimes appears to become oedematous, as another becomes scirrhous, so that a not inconsiderable multitude of compound diseases is also gathered. About these things more has been said both in certain other works and in the books of the Therapeutic Method, and something will be said now as well. At least this much of them it is necessary to recall: the aforementioned poultice would never cure exact erysipelas. I call it exact when the part has been filled by a bilious flux. That coriander is far from cooling you can learn even from what Dioscorides himself wrote. He says, at any rate, that together with crushed pulse (eregmos) it resolves choirades. That none of the cooling drugs is capable of resolving choirades, not even Dioscorides himself, I think, will dispute. For sometimes, when the part that has had the erysipelas has become black, livid and cold, and no longer needs cooling drugs as before, but now needs those that evacuate the humour unnaturally impacted in the region, these people still cool it. At other times they pass on to dispersing drugs, yet they say that they are curing erysipelas. And indeed they also prescribe some drugs while the cases of erysipelas are still beginning and increasing, and others when they are declining. But this is not how things are. For neither should it still be called erysipelas once its fiery, seething and bilious character has gone, nor should the remedies for such conditions be thought cold in their powers. Suppose that right at the start, whether from a blow or in any other way, a livid or black swelling had arisen in some part: it would have been thought to be a cold affection and to need dispersing and heating drugs. In the same way, if a hot condition should at some point change into a cold one, it is right to forget the former and to name the second by another name. Or, if you would not wish to change the name, but, as some do, write some remedies for the beginning and others for the decline, then at least you should not think that the drugs of the decline are also cold. One must grant that someone may call such a condition erysipelas if he wishes, but one must not grant that he still call it hot, once it has been chilled. Let us therefore not think either that what helps it at that time is cooling, as Dioscorides thinks coriander is, because, as he himself says, when applied as a poultice with bread or barley-groats it cures erysipelas. For an exact erysipelas, which is fiery and yellow, coriander with bread would never cure; it cures only one that is already cooling off. For this reason, in the earlier books, when we required that the power of each drug be tested by qualified experience, we advised choosing an affection as simple as possible. But most physicians do not know even that most diseases attack as compound right from the beginning. Nor do they know that exact erysipelas is one affection, and that which is now customarily called by all of us, or at any rate by the ancients, phlegmone is another. In between there are very many others: some one might call phlegmonous cases of erysipelas, others, as it were, certain erysipelatous phlegmonai. You may sometimes also find neither prevailing, but the two exactly balanced. Indeed, erysipelas sometimes appears to become oedematous, as another becomes scirrhous, so that a not inconsiderable multitude of compound diseases is also gathered. About these things more has been said both in certain other works and in the books of the Therapeutic Method, and something will be said now as well. At least this much of them it is necessary to recall: the aforementioned poultice would never cure exact erysipelas. I call it exact when the part has been filled by a bilious flux. That coriander is far from cooling you can learn even from what Dioscorides himself wrote. He says, at any rate, that together with crushed pulse (eregmos) it resolves choirades. That none of the cooling drugs is capable of resolving choirades, not even Dioscorides himself, I think, will dispute. He recorded countless drugs that cure choirades, all of which are agreed to be hot in their mixtures and dispersing in their actions.

[7.12.6] [6. On mastic.] Mastic: the white kind, usually called Chian, is in a way compounded of contrary powers, astringent and softening. For this reason it is suited to inflammations of the stomach, belly, intestines and liver, warming and drying at the second remove. The black kind, called Egyptian, dries more than the former and has less share in the astringent power; hence it is in a way better suited to conditions that require a stronger dispersal. For this reason, at any rate, it is also a good drug for boils. The mastic oil and the mastic unguent, however, are prepared from the Chian kind, and hardly at all from the Egyptian. This too is evidently of a power similar to that of mastic.

raw_text: {"translation": "[7.12.9] [9. On honey.] Honey both dries and heats in the second order. It is of as simple a power and mixture as can be, belonging to the class of drugs that we customarily call cleansing. When boiled, it becomes less pungent and cleansing, which is why people use it for the conglutination of sinuses. [6.1.1] [1. On southernwood and wormwood and the species of each.] Of southernwood, this herb, one need not describe the form, after so many men of such quality, nor its particular actions, since those men set them out, if not with precise distinctions, at least clearly. More will also be said by us about them in the treatise on the composition of drugs and in that on easily procured remedies, and sometimes also in the writings of the Therapeutic Method, when need calls. Only what was proposed from the beginning, to examine the universal powers of all drugs, follows in the case of the others too, and it must now already be done here. It must be said that southernwood is hot and dry in power, ranked somewhere in the third order and remove beyond the balanced state, and has a certain dispersing and cutting power. Of the same power also is its rubbing (?) having taken [it] (τρίψις … εἰληφυῖα), as also the flesh-forming and the biting. That such an order is assessed relative to the well-tempered nature has often been said before. We found out its mixture not least by judging also from taste, for it is quite bitter. Such a flavour was shown to be earthy in its substance and to be thinned by abundant heat, so as both to heat and to dry not feebly. Moreover, having tested it accurately also by the qualified experience, about which it has often been said before, we found this drug to be of the same mixture. For if you pound the foliage together with the flowers (for the rest of it, the dry stalk, is useless) and sprinkle it on a clean ulcer, it appears biting and irritant; and if you steep it in oil and choose to pour it over either the head or the belly, it will be found to heat strongly. And indeed those who are seized by rigors at periods, if you rub them down with it before the onset, shiver less; nor does it escape perception, immediately as it is applied, that it heats. That it is likely to destroy worms, being bitter, is clear even before experience, if we remember anything of what was said in the fourth of these commentaries about the nature of the bitter flavour. You will know at once that it also has a certain dispersing and cutting power. And that this must belong to it more than to wormwood you will be able to infer, first from the taste. For southernwood partakes of a very small acerbity, but wormwood of not a little; and then also from the fact that southernwood is bad for the stomach, as is seriphon too, whereas wormwood is good for the stomach. For it was shown earlier about these things too that the bitter by itself is wholly bad for the stomach, whereas the harsh or acerbic or, in general, the astringent is good for the stomach; and when the qualities are mixed with one another, the stronger would prevail. This, then, is enough for you to know in this treatise. For it will be shown in the writings of the Therapeutic Method how one may best use such a drug. And for this reason do not seek any longer to hear either that, applied as a poultice with boiled quince or with bread, it heals inflammations of the eyes, or that, boiled smooth with ōmēlysis, it disperses phymata. For neither of these nor any of the others is proper to the present treatise; rather, for those who give an empirical teaching it is written in the easily procured drugs, while those who wish to practise the art rationally have need of the Therapeutic Method. For, among other things, one would be harmed rather than benefited by such a report. Now Hippocrates, writing in the Aphorisms, 'pains of the eyes are resolved by drinking of unmixed wine, or a bath, or a vapour-bath, or venesection, or purging', yet not adding what kind of pains drinking of unmixed wine resolves, what kind a bath, which a vapour-bath, which venesection, which purging, one would pardon, I think, for three reasons. For he was giving an aphoristic teaching, in which, because of brevity, many things are allowed to be stated in this way; and he wrote down all the remedies of the pains, even if he did not distinguish which of them suits which kind of pain; or else in many places of his other writings he has given us starting-points for the distinctions in what was stated in this way. But those who have written about such aphorisms neither in other books nor in a detailed and long treatise, but write aphoristically and briefly, and besides this (εἴτε τὸ πρὸς τούτοις) indicate one thing out of many, harm us in more cases than they help. For since there are many differentiae among ophthalmias, and one of them requires the aforementioned poultice while the others are harmed by it, he who uses it on all of them without distinction will harm many more than he helps. In this manner, then, we must write not about southernwood alone but about all the others as well, the powers relating to heating and cooling or moistening or drying being found (εὑρίσκουσιν) by the methods I have often spoken of, but whatever is effected by the peculiarity of the whole substance by experience alone. It has been shown about such things too that they are deleterious, and protective against deleterious things, and purgative. For of these it is not possible to make a rational discovery; rather, it is only possible to find in some cases a certain plausible conjecture, and not indeed in all, just as this very point has been made clear in what precedes. But about the powers found in this way I shall give an account separately in what follows, once I have first gone through, for each species of drug, what concerns heating and cooling, moistening and drying, and whatever follows on these. Having added this much more about southernwood, however, I shall end the discussion: that the most admirable Pamphilus, although writing of this as his first herb, and having perhaps wished, if of none of the following, at least of this one to become an eyewitness, nevertheless erred most greatly, believing that the plant is called santonicum by the Romans. For southernwood differs from santonicum, as Dioscorides too wrote most accurately in the third book On Materials, and all physicians and dealers in small wares (ῥωποπῶλαι) know this at least. For of southernwood there are two species, one considered male, the other female, as this too has been distinguished by Dioscorides and Pamphilus and countless others. Different from it is wormwood, of which again one must posit species, and these threefold: of which one is called wormwood, homonymously with the genus, of which kind especially is the Pontic, another seriphon, another santonicum. But if one should say that wormwood is one thing, seriphon another, and santonicum another, it makes no difference for present purposes. For we have not come to divide a name, but are concerned with the things themselves. Since, then, these are clearly different from one another in form, in taste and in powers, let anyone, if he wishes, name them all by a single appellation, but let him teach their powers accurately. We said, then, that the forms have been described adequately by Dioscorides and not a few others, so that one need not write again what was correctly said by our predecessors. But if those men left anything undistinguished in the powers of this one, for the sake of which indeed I have come to this exposition (ἔξοδον), I shall try to add it. Wormwood is less hot than those mentioned, inasmuch as it partakes of the most astringency. And if it is also less fine-particled than those, it is then in the same way also less thinning than those, yet not less drying. Of the others, santonicum, which has its appellation from the Santonian country in which it grows, is nearest in power to seriphon, falling short by a little in thinning, heating and drying. Seriphon itself is less hot than southernwood but hotter than wormwood, and quite bad for the stomach, as presenting a certain saltiness together with bitterness, and it further partakes a little of acerbity. So too southernwood and santonicum are quite bad for the stomach. For among them wormwood alone, and especially the Pontic, is good for the stomach, because it partakes of the most astringency. Burnt southernwood is hot and dry in power, even more so than burnt dry gourd and dill root. For those suit ulcers that are moist and at the same time calloused without inflammation, and for this reason they seem to be especially in accord with those on the prepuce of the genitals. But the ash of southernwood is biting to all ulcers. And for this reason it suits alopeciae, with a fine-particled oil, namely castor oil or radish oil or Sicyonian or old oil, and especially the Sabine. It also calls forth beards that are slow to come up, with any one of the oils mentioned, and no less than with those when moistened with mastic oil. For it is rarefying, besides being fine-particled, biting and hot; and these are the powers of it that one must especially know, and needs nothing further of the particulars in this treatise.

raw_text: {"translation": "[6.1.2] [2. On agnos or lygos.] Agnos or lygos, the shrubby plant, is hot and drying in about the third remove, and considerably fine-particled; and to the taste the agnos, or lygos, is pungent and at the same time astringent. Its withies (lygoi) themselves it has as useless for medical treatment, but the leaves and the seed are dry and hot in power and fine-particled in substance. For so they appear to those who use them, and to those who taste them the leaf, the flower and the fruit are pungent and at the same time slightly astringent. The fruit is also edible, and it plainly heats, while also being productive of headache. But if it is roasted (for it is eaten in this way too, along with dessert-nibbles), it affects the head less. And it is free of wind in the belly: the unroasted fruit is so, but the roasted still more. Both the roasted and the unroasted fruit also check the impulses towards sexual intercourse, and the leaves and the flowers of the shrub are able to do this same thing, so that they are believed to contribute to chastity not only when eaten and drunk, but also when strewn beneath one. This is why at the Thesmophoria in Athens the women strew the whole shrub beneath themselves, and from this too comes its name. From all of this it is clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding treatises, that agnos heats and at the same time dries, and is most free of wind. That its power is precisely fine-particled, there is evidence. For its affecting the head is reasonably ascribed not to a quantity of vaporous pneuma generated by it, but rather to heat and fineness of particles. The fruit is also edible, and it plainly heats, while also being productive of headache. But if it is roasted (for it is eaten in this way too, along with dessert-nibbles), it affects the head less. And it is free of wind in the belly: the unroasted fruit is so, but the roasted still more. Both the roasted and the unroasted fruit also check the impulses towards sexual intercourse, and the leaves and the flowers of the shrub are able to do this same thing, so that they are believed to contribute to chastity not only when eaten and drunk, but also when strewn beneath one. This is why at the Thesmophoria in Athens the women strew the whole shrub beneath themselves, and from this too comes its name. From all of this it is clear, if we remember what was said in the preceding treatises, that agnos heats and at the same time dries, and is most free of wind. That its power is precisely fine-particled, there is evidence. For its affecting the head is reasonably ascribed not to a quantity of vaporous pneuma generated by it, but rather to heat and fineness of particles. All drugs that are dry together with cooling are suited to malignant ulcers, to fluxes and to putrefactions. On this account they are also suited to dysenteries, for they stop haemorrhages and, if anything is burning hot, they cool it; and they are agglutinating of sinuses and of the other ulcers, fresh and old alike. In nearly all such drugs plantain is either first or second to none in the due proportion of its mixture. For it partakes of a dryness that does not bite and of a coldness not yet numbing. Its fruit and its roots are also of a similar power, except that their power is drier and less cold. But the fruit is more fine-particled, and the roots more coarse-particled. The leaves of the herb themselves, when dried, also come to be of a more fine-particled and less cold power, since the watery residue has breathed out of them and been dispersed. For this reason people use the roots against toothaches as well, chewed and boiled in their mouthwashes. Against obstructions in the liver and kidneys they use these too, but also the leaves, and much more still the fruit. For all of these partake of a certain cleansing power, which is likely to be present in the green herb as well, but to be overcome by the quantity of its moisture.

raw_text: {"translation": "[6.5.4] [4. On oil.] Of oil, the kind that comes from the olive, which we also call oil in the most proper sense, what sort of thing it is in its mixture has been determined in the preceding discussions: it was shown to be moistening and moderately warm. Such is the sweetest oil, produced above all from fruit that has fallen ripe from the tree (drupetēs). The oil called 'raw-pressed' (ōmotribes) and omphacine partakes of cooling to the same extent that it has taken a share of astringency. As for old oil, that which arises from sweet oil growing old is warmer and more dispersing. That which arises from raw-pressed oil is of mixed power so long as it preserves some of its astringency, but when it loses this completely it becomes like the other. Moreover, those who add olive shoots during the preparation also produce an oil similar to omphacine oil. One should not enquire how it has been prepared, but taste it oneself. If it shows some astringency, one should suppose that it shares in cooling to the same extent that it partakes of astringency, as is the case with the oil brought from Iberia, which they call Spanish. But if on tasting it appears not to be astringent at all, and is exactly sweet, one should consider it moderately warm. And if it also appears fine-particled, one should consider it the finest and the one possessing above all the excellence of oil, such as the Sabine is. Fine-particled oil is that which looks pure and translucent, and which, when a small amount is taken, is spread over a very large part of the body, remains continuous with itself, and is drunk up by the skin. That washed oil is the least biting has also been said before. How one might best wash it I shall tell in the following treatise, the one on the composition of drugs; there I shall also speak about Sicyonian oil and any other such oil. For now I am going through the simple drugs, and I shall next add the account of the other oils. raw_text: {"translation": "[6.9.8] [8. On willow.] One might use the leaves of the willow as well for the agglutination of bloody wounds; nevertheless, it is its flower above all that almost all physicians use for the preparation of a drying plaster. For the power of these is drying and non-biting, and it also has astringency. Some also make a juice from them and so obtain a non-biting and drying drug, useful for many purposes. For nothing is of more varied use than a non-biting and drying drug that is slightly astringent, as will be shown more precisely in the books on the composition of drugs. The bark of the tree is also similar to the power of the flowers and of the leaves, except in so far as it is drier in mixture, as indeed are all barks. Some burn this bark and use the ash for whatever needs to be dried strongly. For instance, they remove the so-called nails (corns) and calluses, and also warts, by moistening it with pungent vinegar. Some, incising the bark at the time of flowering, collect a certain sap and use it for things that darken the pupils, as a drug at once cleansing and fine-particled. One might also use it for many other things, since it is of such a kind. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK VIII. Preface. In writing this seventh treatise on the power of simple drugs, we think it necessary to state at the outset that it will be clear only to those who have studied the preceding books, and not as a side matter. The others, I think, will misunderstand rather than learn anything of what is to be said in it; they will go astray themselves, and will perhaps abuse us for writing certain things incorrectly. Those who are sensible, I know, will be persuaded, and if they have cared at all for the theory at hand, they will read the whole treatise from the beginning. But those who are meddlesome rather than eager to learn will disregard this advance notice, and perhaps this is nothing surprising, since some of the uninitiated have even dared to read books of the mysteries. But those who wrote those books did not write them for the profane, nor do I write these for those not yet trained in the first matters. In this book and in the one after it the primary powers of the remaining plants will be stated. Here too we have arranged the order of the teaching according to the order of the letters with which their names begin. In the book before this one we advanced as far as iota; here we shall begin from kappa. First we recall only this much: that we shall refer everything back to the principles demonstrated earlier. For the differences in the particular activities of each drug arise from its being hot or cold, moist or dry, fine-particled or coarse-particled to such-and-such a degree. But how far it advances in each of the aforementioned qualities cannot be expressed, at least with respect to the most precise truth. Yet we have tried to circumscribe this too with clear limits, sufficient for the use of the art. We showed that there is one class of drugs that arrives at a mixture similar to our bodies, once it has received from the heat in them some beginning of change and alteration. There is another class that becomes hotter in relation to us, and of this it seemed good to make four orders. The first is unclear to sense perception, so as to need reason to detect it. response.translation: [6.9.8] [8. On willow.] One might use the leaves of the willow as well for the agglutination of bloody wounds; nevertheless, it is its flower above all that almost all physicians use for the preparation of a drying plaster. For the power of these is drying and non-biting, and it also has astringency. Some also make a juice from them and so obtain a non-biting and drying drug, useful for many purposes. For nothing is of more varied use than a non-biting and drying drug that is slightly astringent, as will be shown more precisely in the books on the composition of drugs. The bark of the tree is also similar to the power of the flowers and of the leaves, except in so far as it is drier in mixture, as indeed are all barks. Some burn this bark and use the ash for whatever needs to be dried strongly. For instance, they remove the so-called nails (corns) and calluses, and also warts, by moistening it with pungent vinegar. Some, incising the bark at the time of flowering, collect a certain sap and use it for things that darken the pupils, as a drug at once cleansing and fine-particled. One might also use it for many other things, since it is of such a kind. GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK VIII. Preface. In writing this seventh treatise on the power of simple drugs, we think it necessary to state at the outset that it will be clear only to those who have studied the preceding books, and not as a side matter. The others, I think, will misunderstand rather than learn anything of what is to be said in it; they will go astray themselves, and will perhaps abuse us for writing certain things incorrectly. Those who are sensible, I know, will be persuaded, and if they have cared at all for the theory at hand, they will read the whole treatise from the beginning. But those who are meddlesome rather than eager to learn will disregard this advance notice, and perhaps this is nothing surprising, since some of the uninitiated have even dared to read books of the mysteries. But those who wrote those books did not write them for the profane, nor do I write these for those not yet trained in the first matters. In this book and in the one after it the primary powers of the remaining plants will be stated. Here too we have arranged the order of the teaching according to the order of the letters with which their names begin. In the book before this one we advanced as far as iota; here we shall begin from kappa. First we recall only this much: that we shall refer everything back to the principles demonstrated earlier. For the differences in the particular activities of each drug arise from its being hot or cold, moist or dry, fine-particled or coarse-particled to such-and-such a degree. But how far it advances in each of the aforementioned qualities cannot be expressed, at least with respect to the most precise truth. Yet we have tried to circumscribe this too with clear limits, sufficient for the use of the art. We showed that there is one class of drugs that arrives at a mixture similar to our bodies, once it has received from the heat in them some beginning of change and alteration. There is another class that becomes hotter in relation to us, and of this it seemed good to make four orders. The first is unclear to sense perception, so as to need reason to detect it. A second follows it, already in some way clear to sense perception. A third heats strongly, yet does not yet in any way burn. After it comes the fourth and last, the caustic. So too with the cooling drugs: the first order is of those that need reason to demonstrate that they cool, the second of those that cool perceptibly, the third of those that cool strongly, and the fourth of those that mortify. The moistening and drying drugs are treated analogously to these.
